title: The Plastic Tide: Ocean Pollution in the Twenty-First Century
source: Adapted from environmental science journals
description: 海洋塑料污染的来源、影响与应对策略
content:
The world's oceans, covering more than seventy percent of the Earth's surface, have long been regarded as the planet's final frontier — a vast, mysterious realm seemingly capable of absorbing and recycling whatever humanity discards into it. This assumption, once taken for granted, has been shattered by a crisis that has unfolded over the past several decades: the contamination of marine environments by plastic waste on a scale that defies comprehension.

The numbers are staggering. According to estimates published by the United Nations Environment Programme, approximately eight million tonnes of plastic enter the oceans each year. This is equivalent to dumping a garbage truck full of plastic into the sea every single minute. By 2050, if current trends continue, the weight of plastic in the oceans could exceed that of all fish combined. Unlike organic materials, which decompose relatively quickly, conventional plastics persist in the marine environment for hundreds of years, fragmenting into ever smaller pieces but never truly disappearing.

The sources of this pollution are diverse, but a handful of rivers are responsible for the lion's share. A study published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology found that just ten river systems — eight in Asia and two in Africa — carry roughly ninety percent of the global input of land-based plastic waste into the oceans. These rivers flow through regions with rapidly growing populations, inadequate waste management infrastructure, and high consumption of single-use packaging. The Yangtze River alone is estimated to transport approximately 1.5 million tonnes of plastic into the East China Sea each year.

Once plastic enters the ocean, it does not remain stationary. Ocean currents, wind, and wave action distribute it across the globe, from the surface waters of tropical seas to the deepest trenches on Earth. In 2018, a team of researchers exploring the Mariana Trench — the deepest known point in the ocean, at a depth of nearly eleven kilometres — discovered plastic bags littering the seafloor. The discovery was a sobering reminder that no corner of the marine environment, however remote, remains untouched by human waste.

The consequences for marine life are profound and multifaceted. Large pieces of plastic pose an immediate physical threat: sea turtles mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish, their primary food source, while seabirds ingest bottle caps and lighters, which accumulate in their stomachs and eventually cause starvation. A study by the Ocean Conservancy found that plastic has been documented in the digestive tracts of over seven hundred marine species, including endangered ones such as the Hawaiian monk seal and the loggerhead turtle.

Equally alarming is the phenomenon of microplastics — plastic fragments smaller than five millimetres in diameter. These tiny particles result from the breakdown of larger items as well as from the direct release of microbeads used in personal care products. Microplastics have been found in every ocean basin on Earth, from the surface to the deep sea, and even in Arctic ice. Because they are small enough to be ingested by plankton and other organisms at the base of the food chain, microplastics bioaccumulate as they move upward, eventually reaching the fish and shellfish that humans consume. A 2019 study commissioned by the World Wildlife Fund estimated that the average person ingests approximately five grams of plastic every week — roughly the equivalent of a credit card — through contaminated food and water.

The chemical dimension of the problem adds another layer of complexity. Plastics are not inert; they contain a range of additives, including plasticisers, flame retardants, and colourants, many of which are known to be toxic. When plastics degrade in seawater, these chemicals are released into the surrounding environment. Moreover, microplastics act like sponges, adsorbing persistent organic pollutants such as PCBs and DDT from the surrounding water. When marine organisms ingest these contaminated particles, the toxins are released into their tissues, where they can disrupt endocrine systems, impair reproduction, and cause developmental abnormalities.

Addressing a problem of this magnitude requires action on multiple fronts. At the international level, there is growing momentum for a legally binding treaty on plastic pollution, akin to the Paris Agreement on climate change. In March 2022, representatives from 175 nations meeting in Nairobi endorsed a resolution to develop such a treaty by 2024, a move widely hailed as the most significant environmental accord since the 2015 climate agreement. The proposed treaty would address the full lifecycle of plastics, from production and design to disposal and recycling.

At the national level, a number of countries have already taken decisive steps. Rwanda, remarkably, banned single-use plastic bags as early as 2008, imposing strict penalties on their manufacture, use, and importation. Kenya followed suit in 2017 with one of the world's most stringent bans, carrying fines of up to $40,000 or prison sentences of up to four years. The European Union's Single-Use Plastics Directive, adopted in 2019, prohibits a range of plastic products — including cutlery, cotton buds, and polystyrene food containers — and requires member states to collect and recycle ninety percent of plastic bottles by 2029.

Technological innovation also plays a critical role. Advances in chemical recycling, which breaks plastics down into their molecular components for reuse, offer the prospect of a truly circular plastics economy. Researchers are also developing biodegradable alternatives derived from plant-based materials such as cornstarch and seaweed. However, these solutions are not without limitations: biodegradable plastics often require specific industrial composting conditions to break down, and scaling up production remains expensive.

Consumer behaviour, ultimately, is perhaps the most powerful lever of all. The choices made by billions of individuals — whether to use a reusable water bottle, to refuse a plastic straw, to purchase products with minimal packaging — collectively shape market demand and, in turn, industrial production. While individual actions alone cannot solve a crisis of this scale, they create the social and economic conditions that make systemic change possible.

The plastic tide, in other words, is not inevitable. It is the product of decisions — by manufacturers, policymakers, and consumers — and it can be reversed by different decisions. What is required is not a single solution but a sustained, coordinated effort across every level of society. The oceans, for all their vastness, have limits, and those limits have been reached. What happens next will depend on whether humanity treats this crisis with the urgency it demands.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of this passage?
options: To compare plastic pollution in different oceans
To provide a comprehensive overview of ocean plastic pollution and potential solutions
To argue that plastic pollution is less serious than climate change
To describe the chemical composition of different plastics
questions.explanation: 文章从污染规模、来源、对海洋生物的影响、微塑料危害、化学毒性、国际/国家/技术/消费者层面的解决方案等多个角度全面阐述了海洋塑料污染问题，因此主旨是 B。A 只涉及一方面，C 与原文立场相反，D 只是一个细节。

questions.question: According to the passage, approximately how much plastic enters the oceans each year?
options: 1.5 million tonnes
5 million tonnes
8 million tonnes
10 million tonnes
questions.explanation: 第二段明确指出 "approximately eight million tonnes of plastic enter the oceans each year"，对应 C。1.5 million tonnes 是长江单独的排放量（第三段），不是全球总量。

questions.question: The study published in Environmental Science & Technology found that approximately what percentage of global land-based plastic waste enters the ocean via just ten rivers?
options: 50 percent
70 percent
80 percent
90 percent
questions.explanation: 第三段原文："just ten river systems... carry roughly ninety percent of the global input of land-based plastic waste into the oceans"，对应 D。

questions.question: The word "adsorbing" in the sixth paragraph is closest in meaning to:
options: dissolving completely
attracting and holding on the surface
breaking down into smaller pieces
repelling and pushing away
questions.explanation: 在原文语境中，微塑料像海绵一样"adsorbing"持久性有机污染物，即在其表面吸附和持留这些化学物质。B"attracting and holding on the surface"最准确。A 是溶解，C 是分解，D 是排斥，均不符合语境。

questions.question: What can be inferred about biodegradable plastics from the passage?
options: They are the definitive solution to ocean plastic pollution
They can break down naturally in any marine environment
They have limitations, including requiring specific conditions and being costly to produce
They are already widely used and have replaced conventional plastics
questions.explanation: 第八段指出："these solutions are not without limitations: biodegradable plastics often require specific industrial composting conditions to break down, and scaling up production remains expensive"，C 准确概括了这两点局限。A 和 B 与原文相反，D 与原文不符（还在发展中）。

questions.question: The author's overall tone in this passage can best be described as:
options: Optimistic and dismissive of the problem
Objective and concerned, with a call to action
Angry and accusatory toward specific countries
Indifferent and purely academic
questions.explanation: 作者用大量数据和事实客观呈现问题（concerned），最后以"What is required is... a sustained, coordinated effort"结尾呼吁行动（call to action），但并未愤怒指责特定国家或漠不关心。B 最准确。

title: The Silicon Workforce: How Artificial Intelligence Is Reshaping Employment
source: Adapted from technology and economics publications
description: 人工智能对就业市场的冲击、机遇与未来趋势
content:
In March 2023, the investment bank Goldman Sachs published a report that sent shockwaves through boardrooms and government ministries alike. The study concluded that generative artificial intelligence — the technology behind systems such as ChatGPT — could automate tasks equivalent to roughly three hundred million full-time jobs worldwide. Within a decade, the report suggested, two-thirds of occupations in the United States and Europe would be exposed to some degree of automation by AI. The headline was dramatic, but beneath it lay a far more nuanced reality that demands careful examination.

To understand the impact of AI on employment, it is helpful to distinguish between jobs and tasks. A job is a collection of tasks; AI rarely replaces an entire job outright. Instead, it automates specific tasks within a job, transforming how the work is done rather than eliminating the person who does it. A lawyer, for instance, may spend hours reviewing contracts for specific clauses — a task that AI can now perform in seconds. But the lawyer's broader role — advising clients, negotiating settlements, arguing in court — remains distinctly human, at least for the foreseeable future. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report, published in 2023, estimated that while AI and automation could displace approximately eighty-three million jobs globally by 2027, they would also create sixty-nine million new ones — a net loss of fourteen million, or roughly two percent of current employment.

Historically, this pattern of destruction and creation is not new. The Industrial Revolution eliminated countless agricultural and artisanal jobs, but it generated entire industries that employed far more people at higher wages. The advent of the personal computer destroyed typewriter manufacturing and entire categories of clerical work, yet it gave rise to a software industry that now employs tens of millions worldwide. The economist Joseph Schumpeter coined the term "creative destruction" to describe this process, arguing that it is the essential engine of economic progress. AI, its proponents argue, is simply the latest iteration of a phenomenon that has been reshaping labour markets for two centuries.

This analogy, however, has its limits. Previous waves of automation primarily replaced physical labour, freeing humans to pursue cognitive work. AI, by contrast, is automating cognitive work itself — writing, analysing, summarising, even creative tasks such as graphic design and music composition. This raises a question that previous generations did not face: if machines can perform both manual and intellectual tasks, what is left for humans to do?

The answer, according to most labour economists, lies in the qualities that remain stubbornly difficult to automate. Empathy, for instance, is a capacity that no algorithm can genuinely replicate, however convincingly a chatbot may simulate concern. A nurse comforting a frightened patient, a teacher reading a child's frustration, a social worker building trust with a vulnerable family — these are tasks that require not just knowledge but genuine human connection. Similarly, tasks involving complex physical dexterity in unpredictable environments — plumbing, electrical repair, construction — remain extraordinarily difficult for robots to perform reliably. The philosopher Hubert Dreyfus argued decades ago that true intelligence is embodied, rooted in physical experience and social context, and that purely computational systems would always struggle with tasks that humans perform intuitively.

Moreover, AI is creating entirely new categories of employment that did not exist a decade ago. Prompt engineers — specialists who design and refine the inputs given to AI systems to elicit useful outputs — command salaries exceeding three hundred thousand dollars in Silicon Valley. AI ethicists, data curators, machine learning auditors, and algorithmic bias testers are all roles that have emerged in direct response to the proliferation of AI. The World Economic Forum identified AI and machine learning specialists as the fastest-growing job category globally, projecting thirty percent growth over five years.

The challenge, then, is not so much a lack of jobs as a mismatch between the skills that workers currently possess and those that the new economy demands. This mismatch is particularly acute for workers in middle-skill occupations — bookkeepers, data entry clerks, assembly line workers — whose tasks are most susceptible to automation. A study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development found that workers without tertiary education are three to four times more likely to be displaced by automation than those with university degrees. The result, if left unaddressed, is a widening inequality gap: highly educated workers reap the benefits of the AI revolution, while those with fewer qualifications face stagnation or decline.

Bridging this gap requires a fundamental rethinking of education and training systems. Traditional models, in which individuals complete their education in their early twenties and rely on that knowledge for the remainder of their careers, are increasingly inadequate in a world where the half-life of technical skills is estimated at just two and a half years. Continuous, lifelong learning is no longer a luxury but a necessity. Countries such as Singapore have pioneered national skills-development programmes — the SkillsFuture initiative, for example, provides every citizen with training credits that can be used throughout their working lives. Denmark's flexicurity model, which combines flexible labour markets (making it relatively easy for employers to hire and fire) with robust social safety nets and active retraining programmes, offers another template.

Governments also face difficult questions about regulation. The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, provisionally agreed in December 2023, represents the world's first comprehensive legal framework for AI. It classifies AI systems by risk level, banning those deemed to pose "unacceptable risk" — such as social scoring systems — and imposing strict requirements on "high-risk" applications, including those used in recruitment, education, and law enforcement. Critics argue that such regulation may stifle innovation; proponents counter that public trust, fostered by sensible oversight, is itself a prerequisite for widespread adoption.

The transformative potential of AI in the workplace is undeniable. It promises productivity gains that could boost global GDP by seven percent over a decade, according to Goldman Sachs. AI-powered diagnostic tools are already improving the accuracy and speed of medical diagnoses. Automated translation is breaking down language barriers in international commerce. Predictive analytics are helping farmers optimise crop yields and reducing food waste. These are not trivial benefits.

Yet the distribution of those benefits is not predetermined. Left to market forces alone, AI is likely to concentrate wealth in the hands of those who own and control the technology, while hollowing out the middle of the income distribution. Whether AI becomes a force for shared prosperity or deepening inequality depends on choices — about education, regulation, social safety nets, and the values embedded in the technology itself — that societies must make deliberately and soon. The machines are here. The question is whether humanity will shape them, or be shaped by them.

questions.question: According to the Goldman Sachs report mentioned in the first paragraph, approximately how many full-time jobs could generative AI automate worldwide?
options: 69 million
83 million
300 million
2 percent of all jobs
questions.explanation: 第一段原文："generative artificial intelligence... could automate tasks equivalent to roughly three hundred million full-time jobs worldwide"。69 million 和 83 million 是世界经济论坛报告中的新增和消失岗位数（第二段），2% 是净损失比例。

questions.question: The author uses the example of the lawyer in the second paragraph primarily to illustrate that:
options: AI will soon replace all lawyers completely
AI automates specific tasks within a job rather than replacing the entire job
Lawyers are among the most threatened professionals
Contract review is the only task AI can perform in law
questions.explanation: 第二段明确区分了"job"和"task"，用律师的例子说明AI自动化的是任务（审阅合同条款），而非整个职业（律师还要为客户提供咨询、谈判、法庭辩护等），因此 B 正确。A 与原文"remains distinctly human"矛盾，C 和 D 过于绝对。

questions.question: What is a key difference between previous waves of automation and the AI revolution, according to the passage?
options: Previous automation created more jobs than it destroyed, while AI will only destroy jobs
Previous automation primarily replaced physical labour, while AI is automating cognitive work
Previous automation happened faster, while AI adoption is slower
Previous automation affected only developed countries, while AI affects all countries equally
questions.explanation: 第四段明确指出："Previous waves of automation primarily replaced physical labour, freeing humans to pursue cognitive work. AI, by contrast, is automating cognitive work itself — writing, analysing, summarising, even creative tasks"。B 准确概括了这一关键区别。A 错（AI也会创造新岗位），C 和 D 原文未提及。

questions.question: The phrase "creative destruction" in the third paragraph refers to:
options: The damage caused by AI to creative industries
The process by which old jobs are destroyed and new ones created, driving economic progress
The destruction of physical products by digital alternatives
The negative impact of technology on workplace creativity
questions.explanation: 第三段引用经济学家熊彼特的概念"creative destruction"，随后解释其为"the essential engine of economic progress"，即旧岗位被摧毁、新岗位被创造的过程。B 准确。A、C、D 都曲解了原文含义。

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a quality that remains difficult for AI to automate?
options: Empathy and genuine human connection
Complex physical dexterity in unpredictable environments
Speed of processing large datasets
Tasks rooted in physical experience and social context
questions.explanation: 第五段提到 empathy（A）、physical dexterity in unpredictable environments（B）和 Dreyfus 的"embodied intelligence"理论（D）都是难以自动化的。C"大规模数据处理速度"恰恰是 AI 擅长的，不是"难以自动化"的品质，因此答案是 C。

questions.question: What does the author suggest is the most significant challenge regarding AI and employment?
options: A complete lack of new job creation
The mismatch between workers' current skills and the skills the new economy demands
The refusal of governments to regulate AI at all
The inability of AI to improve productivity
questions.explanation: 第七段明确指出："The challenge, then, is not so much a lack of jobs as a mismatch between the skills that workers currently possess and those that the new economy demands"。B 准确。A 与原文矛盾（新岗位正在创造），C 过于绝对（欧盟已在立法），D 与原文"productivity gains"矛盾。

title: The Urban Surge: How City Growth Is Reshaping Society
source: Adapted from urban studies and development publications
description: 全球城市化进程的驱动因素、挑战与可持续发展方向
content:
In 2007, for the first time in human history, more than half of the world's population lived in cities. By 2050, according to projections from the United Nations, that figure will rise to nearly seventy percent. The urban population, currently around 4.5 billion, is expected to approach seven billion within three decades. This transformation — the largest migration in human history — is reshaping not only where people live, but how they live, work, interact, and govern themselves.

The drivers of urbanisation are well understood. In developing nations, the primary force is rural-to-urban migration, fuelled by the search for economic opportunity. A farmer in Bangladesh earning two dollars a day can earn five times that amount in a garment factory in Dhaka. In developed nations, urban growth is driven less by migration and more by the concentration of high-value economic activity — finance, technology, research — in metropolitan areas that offer the dense networks of talent and capital that modern industries require. The economist Edward Glaeser has called cities "humanity's greatest invention," arguing that density fosters innovation, productivity, and creativity in ways that dispersed settlement patterns cannot match.

Yet the very density that makes cities engines of prosperity also generates extraordinary challenges. Housing is perhaps the most acute. In London, the median house price now exceeds twelve times the median annual income; in Hong Kong, the ratio is an astonishing twenty-one. The result is a generation of urban residents who are effectively priced out of homeownership, condemned to spend disproportionate shares of their income on rent or to endure long commutes from increasingly distant peripheries. In the developing world, the housing crisis takes a different form: the proliferation of informal settlements, or slums, where an estimated one billion people currently live without adequate sanitation, clean water, or secure land tenure.

Transportation presents a parallel challenge. As cities grow, the distance between where people live and where they work increases, placing enormous strain on infrastructure. Traffic congestion in megacities such as Jakarta, Manila, and Lagos costs billions in lost productivity each year. In Lagos, Nigeria's commercial capital, the average commuter spends an estimated thirty hours per week in traffic — nearly the equivalent of a full working day. The environmental consequences are equally severe: urban transport accounts for roughly forty percent of transport-related carbon emissions globally, and the air pollution it generates contributes to millions of premature deaths annually.

The response to these challenges has taken various forms. Some cities have invested heavily in public transit. Tokyo's rail network, widely regarded as the most efficient in the world, carries over eight million passengers daily with an average delay of less than one minute per train. Bogotá's TransMilenio bus rapid transit system, launched in 2000, demonstrated that world-class public transport is achievable even in cities of the Global South, reducing commute times by nearly a third and inspiring similar systems in dozens of cities worldwide. Cycling infrastructure, once dismissed as impractical in large cities, has become a priority: Copenhagen's cycling network now handles more journeys than its public transit system, with sixty-two percent of residents commuting to work or school by bicycle.

A more recent development is the concept of the "smart city" — the use of data, sensors, and digital technology to optimise urban services. Singapore, often cited as the world's leading smart city, uses a network of sensors to monitor traffic flow, adjust traffic signals in real time, and predict congestion before it occurs. Barcelona's smart water management system, which uses sensors to detect leaks and optimise irrigation in public parks, has reduced water consumption by twenty-five percent. In Songdo, South Korea, a city built from scratch as a smart city experiment, pneumatic waste collection systems eliminate the need for garbage trucks, while telepresence screens in every home connect residents to government services.

Yet the smart city vision has its critics. Privacy advocates warn that the proliferation of surveillance technology — cameras, facial recognition, licence plate readers — risks creating what Shoshana Zuboff, a Harvard Business School professor, has termed "surveillance capitalism," in which the data generated by urban life is harvested and monetised, often without the knowledge or consent of residents. In 2018, a leaked document revealed that Sidewalk Labs, a subsidiary of Google's parent company Alphabet, had proposed building a sensor-laden neighbourhood on Toronto's waterfront — a project that was eventually abandoned in 2020 amid public backlash over data governance concerns. The episode highlighted a fundamental tension: the technologies that promise to make cities more efficient also threaten to make them less free.

There is also the question of who benefits from urban innovation. Smart city technologies tend to be deployed first in affluent neighbourhoods, where infrastructure is already robust and residents have the political voice to demand improvement. Low-income areas, where the need is often greatest, are frequently left waiting. In Mumbai, the city's first metro line, opened in 2014, serves the affluent western suburbs; the densely populated eastern neighbourhoods, home to many of the city's poorest residents, remain dependent on overcrowded suburban trains. The risk is that technology exacerbates rather than ameliorates urban inequality.

Perhaps the most promising approach is one that does not rely on technology alone. The concept of the "fifteen-minute city," popularised by the urban planner Carlos Moreno, envisions neighbourhoods in which most daily needs — work, shopping, education, healthcare, recreation — are accessible within a fifteen-minute walk or bicycle ride. Paris, under Mayor Anne Hidalgo, has adopted this concept as the guiding principle of its urban planning, converting roads to bicycle lanes, repurposing parking spaces, and decentralising public services. The appeal of the fifteen-minute city lies in its simplicity: it does not require sensors or algorithms, only thoughtful design and political will.

The urban surge of the coming decades is, in one sense, inevitable. The question is not whether cities will grow but whether they will grow well — whether they become places of opportunity and flourishing for all their residents, or places of division, congestion, and environmental degradation. The answer will depend not on any single technology or policy, but on the willingness of societies to invest in people as much as in infrastructure, to prioritise equity as much as efficiency, and to remember that a city, at its best, is not merely a machine for living but a community for thriving.

questions.question: According to the passage, approximately how many people currently live in cities worldwide?
options: 2.5 billion
4.5 billion
7 billion
Over 10 billion
questions.explanation: 第一段原文："The urban population, currently around 4.5 billion, is expected to approach seven billion within three decades"。7 billion 是2050年预计值，B 是当前值。

questions.question: What does Edward Glaeser mean when he calls cities "humanity's greatest invention"?
options: Cities are the most technologically advanced human creation
Cities foster innovation, productivity, and creativity through density
Cities are the only place where economic growth can occur
Cities were the first form of human settlement
questions.explanation: 第二段原文：Glaeser "arguing that density fosters innovation, productivity, and creativity in ways that dispersed settlement patterns cannot match"，即城市的密度促进了创新、生产力和创造力。B 准确。A、C、D 都曲解了原意。

questions.question: In Hong Kong, the ratio of median house price to median annual income is approximately:
options: 8 times
12 times
15 times
21 times
questions.explanation: 第三段原文："in Hong Kong, the ratio is an astonishing twenty-one"。12 times 是伦敦的比例。D 正确。

questions.question: The example of Lagos is used in the passage to illustrate:
options: The success of smart city technology in Africa
The severe impact of traffic congestion on urban productivity
The effectiveness of public transit systems in developing nations
The housing crisis in informal settlements
questions.explanation: 第四段用拉各斯的例子说明交通拥堵的严重性："the average commuter spends an estimated thirty hours per week in traffic"，强调生产力损失。B 正确。A 与原文不符（拉各斯不是智慧城市案例），C 相反，D 是第三段的内容（贫民窟住房问题），与拉各斯交通例子无关。

questions.question: What happened to the Sidewalk Labs project in Toronto?
options: It was successfully completed and became a model for other cities
It was modified to exclude all surveillance technology
It was abandoned amid public backlash over data governance concerns
It was relocated to Songdo, South Korea
questions.explanation: 第七段原文："a project that was eventually abandoned in 2020 amid public backlash over data governance concerns"。Sidewalk Labs 因公众对数据治理的强烈反对而被放弃。C 正确。

questions.question: The "fifteen-minute city" concept described in the passage is notable because it:
options: Relies entirely on advanced AI and sensor technology
Was first implemented in Singapore
Does not require technology, only thoughtful design and political will
Focuses on reducing urban population density
questions.explanation: 第九段原文："The appeal of the fifteen-minute city lies in its simplicity: it does not require sensors or algorithms, only thoughtful design and political will"。十五分钟城市不需要技术，只需周到的设计和政治意愿。C 正确。A 相反，B 错（是巴黎），D 错（不是减少密度）。

title: The Vanishing Canopy: Deforestation and the Fight to Save Rainforests
source: Adapted from environmental science and conservation publications
description: 热带雨林砍伐的动因、生态后果与保护努力
content:
Rainforests are among the most ancient and biologically richest ecosystems on the planet, yet they are disappearing at a rate that alarmed scientists long before it captured public attention. Covering roughly six percent of the Earth's land surface, tropical rainforests are home to more than half of all known terrestrial species. Yet according to estimates from the Food and Agriculture Organization, the world loses around ten million hectares of forest cover each year, an area roughly the size of Iceland. The greater part of this loss occurs in the tropics, where the canopy that once formed a continuous green carpet is being fragmented into isolated patches. The phrase 'the vanishing canopy' is therefore not merely poetic; it describes a measurable, accelerating retreat with consequences that reach far beyond the countries in which the trees once stood.

The geography of this retreat is uneven but concentrated. Three regions dominate the story. The Amazon basin, stretching across nine South American nations, holds the largest single expanse of tropical forest and absorbs an enormous quantity of carbon each year. The Congo Basin in Central Africa is the second largest, and the forests of Southeast Asia, especially in Indonesia and Malaysia, are the most rapidly exploited. In each region the pattern is similar: an initial road or track opens the frontier, settlers and commercial operators follow, and within a few years a landscape of immense complexity is converted into pasture, monoculture plantation, or scrub. Satellite imagery assembled over four decades shows that the arc of deforestation, a sweeping curve of cleared land along the southern and eastern edges of the Amazon, has become the most visible symbol of the phenomenon.

Understanding why forests are cleared is essential to understanding how the process might be slowed. The drivers are rarely simple acts of wanton destruction; they are usually embedded in economic incentives and global supply chains. Cattle ranching is the single largest cause of deforestation in the Amazon, accounting for roughly eighty percent of cleared land in some estimates. Vast herds are raised on land that was recently forest, and much of the beef enters international markets. Soy cultivation is another major force, with Brazil now one of the world's largest producers; the crop is grown largely for animal feed, so a demand for meat thousands of kilometres away can be translated directly into cleared hectares. In Southeast Asia, palm oil plantations have expanded spectacularly because the crop is exceptionally productive and appears in everything from margarine to shampoo.

Logging, both legal and illegal, forms a further strand of the problem. Selective logging may appear less damaging than clear-cutting, but it opens the canopy to sunlight and dries out the forest floor, making the remaining vegetation vulnerable to fire. Roads built to extract timber also provide access for farmers and speculators, so a single logging concession can trigger a much wider wave of clearing. Illegal logging is especially difficult to control because timber is easily disguised and documents are easily forged. The result is a market in which responsible operators struggle to compete with those who ignore the rules, and the forest pays the price.

The most immediate ecological consequence of deforestation is the loss of habitat. A tropical forest is not a uniform collection of trees but a layered architecture, from the emergent crowns high above to the shaded understory and the rich litter of the forest floor. Each layer supports distinct communities of insects, birds, mammals, and plants, many of which are found nowhere else. When the canopy is removed, this architecture collapses. Studies in the Amazon have shown that bird and butterfly diversity can fall by more than half in fragmented forest patches, and that species with narrow ranges disappear first. Because tropical species often have small populations and specialized needs, local extinctions can accumulate rapidly, and once lost, a species cannot be restored by replanting trees alone.

Deforestation also alters the global climate in two distinct ways. First, trees are enormous storehouses of carbon: a mature rainforest may hold more than a hundred tonnes of carbon per hectare in its wood, roots, and soil. When forest is burned or left to rot, much of that carbon returns to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. Second, a living forest continues to absorb carbon through photosynthesis, acting as a sink that offsets a portion of human emissions. The destruction of forest therefore both adds emissions and removes a mechanism that would have absorbed them. Scientists estimate that deforestation and forest degradation together account for roughly ten percent of global carbon emissions, a contribution comparable to that of the entire transport sector.

Beyond carbon, forests regulate water in ways that are only now being fully appreciated. Through transpiration, a large rainforest releases vast quantities of water vapour into the atmosphere, effectively generating its own rainfall. In the Amazon, researchers have described airborne rivers of moisture, bands of humid air that carry water from the forest toward agricultural regions far to the south. When the forest is reduced, this recycling weakens, rainfall declines, and droughts become more likely. Computer models suggest that extensive clearing could push parts of the Amazon toward a drier savanna-like state, a shift that would be extremely difficult to reverse. The irony is that agricultural interests often clear the forest to create farmland, only to find that the regional climate on which farming depends has been undermined.

The soil of tropical forests is another casualty of clearing. Contrary to popular assumption, rainforest soils are often poor in nutrients; the fertility of the ecosystem resides mainly in the living biomass and in the thin layer of decomposing organic matter at the surface. Heavy rain rapidly leaches nutrients once the protective canopy is gone, and the exposed soil is easily eroded. Within a few seasons, cleared land that produced a harvest may be exhausted, prompting farmers to abandon it and move deeper into the forest. Soil scientists know that maintaining ground cover and recycling organic matter are essential if tropical soils are to remain productive over the long term.

The human dimensions of deforestation are equally serious. Indigenous peoples and traditional communities have inhabited tropical forests for millennia and often manage them with sophisticated knowledge of planting, hunting, and fire. For these groups the forest is not an obstacle to development but the foundation of their livelihoods, medicine, and cultural identity. When land is grabbed or degraded, communities lose not only income but also the ecological knowledge that has allowed them to live sustainably. Conservation policies that simply exclude people from forests can therefore be both unjust and ineffective. A growing body of evidence indicates that forests with secure indigenous land tenure are often better protected than state-managed reserves, because local communities have both the incentive and the detailed knowledge to defend them.

In response to these challenges, a range of conservation strategies has emerged. Protected areas remain the cornerstone: today roughly fifteen percent of the world's forest area lies within some form of protected designation. Yet designation on a map is not the same as protection on the ground, and many reserves suffer from underfunding and weak enforcement. A more recent approach, known as payments for ecosystem services, attempts to make standing forests economically valuable. Under schemes such as REDD+, which stands for Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation, wealthy countries and companies provide funds to developing nations that keep forests intact, treating the stored carbon as a service worth purchasing. Early results are mixed, but the approach has at least begun to shift the calculation that makes clearing appear more profitable than conservation.

Technology is also reshaping the fight to save forests. Satellites now provide near-real-time imagery of forest cover, allowing authorities to detect new clearings within days rather than years. In Brazil, a monitoring system combined with strict enforcement helped reduce Amazon deforestation by more than seventy percent between 2004 and 2012, a striking demonstration that political will can matter as much as money. Drones are used to patrol remote reserves and to map illegal logging roads, while acoustic sensors can detect the sound of chainsaws in otherwise inaccessible terrain. Together these tools make it harder for destruction to proceed unnoticed.

Despite such progress, the forces driving deforestation remain powerful, and the outcome is far from certain. Rising global demand for beef, soy, palm oil, and timber continues to create pressure on forest frontiers, while weak governance and corruption can undermine even well-designed policies. The most promising path therefore combines strict protection of high-value forest with support for sustainable livelihoods, secure land rights for indigenous peoples, and supply-chain reforms that make deforestation-free products the norm rather than the exception. The canopy is vanishing, but the past two decades have shown that the trend is not inevitable. Whether the remaining forests survive will depend less on scientific uncertainty than on the willingness of consumers, governments, and companies to act on what is already known.

questions.question: What is the central argument of this passage?
options: Rainforests can be fully restored within a decade once logging stops
Deforestation is driven by economic forces but can be slowed by combining protection, technology and incentives
Tropical soils are too poor to support any form of agriculture whatsoever
Indigenous peoples are the principal cause of forest loss in the tropics
questions.explanation: 全文先分析砍伐动因（牛肉、大豆、棕榈油、 logging），再讲生态与气候后果，最后给出保护区、REDD+、卫星监测等对策，并在末段总结需多管齐下，故主旨为 B。A 原文从未声称十年可恢复；C 过于绝对，原文说土壤贫瘠但可通过保持覆盖持续生产；D 与原文相反，原文认为原住民往往是森林最好的守护者。

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the single largest cause of deforestation in the Amazon?
options: Palm oil plantations
Illegal logging
Cattle ranching
Soy cultivation
questions.explanation: 第3段明确写道 'Cattle ranching is the single largest cause of deforestation in the Amazon, accounting for roughly eighty percent of cleared land'，故选 C。A 棕榈油主要与东南亚相关；B 非法 logging 是重要因素但非单一最大原因；D 大豆是主要力量之一，但原文明确指出最大原因仍是养牛。

questions.question: What does the passage say about payments for ecosystem services such as REDD+?
options: They pay developing countries to keep forests standing by treating stored carbon as a valuable service
They have completely eliminated deforestation in all participating countries
They are designed mainly to expand the boundaries of protected areas
They provide funding exclusively for satellite monitoring systems
questions.explanation: 第10段说明 REDD+ 由富裕国家和企业提供资金给保持森林完整的发展中国家，把储存的碳视为可购买的服务，故 A 正确。B '完全消除' 与原文 'Early results are mixed' 矛盾；C 错，它不是为了扩大保护区边界；D 错，资金并非专用于卫星监测。

questions.question: The word 'leaches' in the passage (paragraph about soil) is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: restores
measures
absorbs
washes away
questions.explanation: 原文语境为 'Heavy rain rapidly leaches nutrients once the protective canopy is gone, and the exposed soil is easily eroded'，指雨水把养分淋溶、冲走，与 'washes away' 同义，故选 D。A 恢复、B 测量、C 吸收均不符合 'leach'（淋洗、滤去）的词义，且与后文土壤被侵蚀的逻辑不符。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the 'airborne rivers of moisture' mentioned in the passage?
options: They are a new technology for measuring rainfall
Their weakening would probably reduce rainfall and threaten agriculture far from the forest
They occur only in the Congo Basin
They increase the rate of carbon emissions from burning forests
questions.explanation: 第7段说这些水汽带把水分从森林输送到遥远的农业区，森林减少时这种循环减弱、降雨减少、干旱更可能，由此可推断其减弱会减少降雨并威胁远处农业，故 B 正确。A 把它们误认为技术；C 原文说的是亚马逊；D 与碳排放无关。

questions.question: What is the author's attitude toward the future of tropical rainforests?
options: Certain that all remaining forest will inevitably disappear
Completely indifferent to the outcome
Cautiously hopeful that the decline can be reversed
Openly hostile toward conservation organizations
questions.explanation: 末段说 'the trend is not inevitable'，并指出过去二十年证明政治意愿可以大幅减少砍伐，说明作者持谨慎乐观态度，故 C 正确。A 与 'not inevitable' 直接矛盾；B 作者大量论述紧迫性，显然并非漠不关心；D 原文对保护组织并无敌意。

title: A Warming World: Climate Change and the Rise of Extreme Weather
source: Adapted from climate science and atmospheric research publications
description: 气候变化与极端天气的关联及科学证据
content:
For much of human history, the weather was treated as a force beyond explanation, a series of random events sent by gods or chance. That view has changed profoundly. Scientists now understand that while no single storm or heatwave can be attributed to climate change in a simple, direct sense, the statistical backdrop against which weather occurs has shifted. The result is a world in which certain kinds of extreme weather are becoming more frequent, more intense, or both. The connection between a gradually warming planet and the violent weather that dominates news headlines is one of the most consequential scientific questions of our time, and the evidence for it has grown from a matter of inference into a body of detailed, quantitative proof.

The physical foundation of the argument is well established. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat in the atmosphere, and human activities have raised their concentrations to levels unseen for at least two million years. Measurements taken at Mauna Loa since the late 1950s show carbon dioxide climbing steadily past 400 parts per million, while the global average temperature has risen by roughly 1.2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. This may sound modest, but a small shift in the average of a distribution can produce a large change in the frequency of extremes. A useful analogy is to imagine a bell curve of daily temperatures being nudged to the right: events that once lay far out in the tail become part of ordinary experience, and events that were once almost unimaginable move within reach.

Rising average temperatures have made heatwaves longer, hotter, and more common. The European heatwave of 2003, which claimed tens of thousands of lives, was for years regarded as an exceptional anomaly; subsequent research concluded that climate change had roughly doubled the likelihood of such an event occurring. A similar event in the Pacific Northwest of North America in 2021 shattered temperature records by extraordinary margins, with some stations reporting readings more than four degrees Celsius above their previous all-time highs. In cities, the effect is intensified by the urban heat island phenomenon, where concrete and asphalt absorb heat by day and release it at night. Heat is therefore not only a meteorological issue but an urban-planning and public-health challenge, particularly for older people and those without access to cooling.

Warming also dries the landscape, lengthening fire seasons and increasing the severity of droughts. Higher temperatures accelerate evaporation from soil and vegetation, so even regions where rainfall does not decline substantially can experience drier conditions on the ground. Australia's catastrophic bushfire season of 2019 and 2020 burned an area larger than many countries, destroyed thousands of homes, and produced smoke that affected air quality across the continent and beyond. In the western United States, a combination of chronic drought, heat, and accumulated fuel has produced fire seasons that now begin earlier and end later than they did a generation ago. The ecological consequences extend beyond the immediate destruction, since forests that burn too frequently may fail to regenerate and can convert permanently to scrubland.

At the opposite extreme, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, a relationship described by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, which implies roughly seven percent more water vapour for every degree Celsius of warming. This additional moisture must eventually fall, and it does so in increasingly intense bursts. Studies of daily rainfall records show that the heaviest precipitation events have intensified in many parts of the world, even where total rainfall has not increased. The consequence is a paradox in flood risk: soils may be drier between storms yet less able to absorb the sudden deluge when it arrives, so flooding can worsen alongside drought. Urban areas, with their vast expanses of impermeable surface, are especially vulnerable, since storm drains and rivers designed for earlier rainfall totals are overwhelmed.

Tropical cyclones present a more complicated picture. The total number of storms globally has not clearly increased, and in some basins may even have decreased. However, a larger proportion now reach the most severe categories, and storms are more likely to undergo rapid intensification, strengthening dramatically in a matter of hours. This is because warm ocean water is the fuel of such systems, and rising sea surface temperatures provide more energy. Storm surge damage is also amplified by sea-level rise, which raises the baseline from which waves push inland. For coastal communities, the combined effect of stronger storms, higher seas, and heavier rainfall creates a compound threat that no single line of defence can fully address.

One of the most important developments in recent decades is the emergence of attribution science, a field that seeks to quantify the role of climate change in specific events. Rather than asking whether an event was 'caused' by climate change, researchers construct counterfactual models of a world without human-emitted greenhouse gases and compare the probability or intensity of the event in that world with the one we inhabit. Using this approach, teams have concluded that climate change made a recent heatwave in India roughly thirty times more likely, or that it increased the rainfall from a particular hurricane by a measurable percentage. Such studies transform an abstract global trend into statements about particular disasters, and they are increasingly cited in legal cases, insurance assessments, and adaptation planning.

Extreme events rarely occur in isolation, and the most dangerous situations arise when hazards combine. A heatwave and drought occurring together can destroy harvests while simultaneously increasing energy demand for cooling, straining the electricity grid just when it is needed most. A storm striking after weeks of heavy rain causes worse flooding because the ground is already saturated. Scientists use the term compound events for such combinations, and they note that the interactions are often more damaging than the sum of the individual hazards. Cascading risks are equally concerning: a cyberattack or equipment failure during a heat emergency can disable the very systems that protect people, revealing how tightly modern infrastructure is interdependent.

The burden of these impacts is profoundly unequal. Wealthy nations have generally contributed the most to historical emissions, yet poorer countries often suffer the worst consequences because they possess fewer resources for protection and recovery. Within cities, low-income neighbourhoods tend to have less tree cover, poorer housing, and limited access to air conditioning, making them hotter during heatwaves and more prone to flooding. Older adults, young children, people with chronic illnesses, and outdoor workers face elevated risks. The farmer losing a harvest to drought and the insurer paying out after a flood experience the same physical event through very different circumstances, and this disparity raises difficult questions of justice that sit alongside the scientific ones.

The economic costs are already substantial and are projected to grow. Insurers have withdrawn from some high-risk markets as payouts for weather-related losses have risen, and governments are increasingly called upon to act as insurers of last resort. Repeated disasters can trap regions in a cycle of rebuilding that leaves little room for long-term investment. Agricultural yields become less predictable, threatening food security, while heat and humidity reduce labour productivity in sectors ranging from construction to manufacturing. Mass displacement is another emerging consequence, as communities in some low-lying or drought-prone regions find that staying is no longer viable. These economic effects are not separate from the physical science; they are the pathway through which changing weather enters everyday life.

Responses fall into two broad categories: mitigation, which aims to reduce the emissions driving the trend, and adaptation, which reduces vulnerability to the changes already under way. Mitigation requires a rapid transition away from fossil fuels, improvements in energy efficiency, and the protection of natural carbon sinks such as forests. Adaptation includes early-warning systems, heat action plans, flood-defence infrastructure, drought-resistant crops, and the restoration of wetlands that can absorb excess water. Neither approach alone is sufficient. Because some additional warming is already locked in by past emissions, adaptation is unavoidable; but without deep mitigation, the scale of adaptation eventually becomes impossible. The most effective strategies combine both, and they work best when they are planned at the regional level rather than improvised after disasters.

The science of extreme weather has reached a point where the debate has shifted. The question for researchers is no longer whether climate change is influencing extremes, but how much, where, and with what consequences for particular communities. That shift has practical importance, because it allows governments and businesses to plan on the basis of evidence rather than argument. Heatwaves, droughts, floods, and intensified storms are not a distant forecast; they are features of the present. How severe they become in the decades ahead will depend in large measure on choices made now about emissions, infrastructure, and the protection of the most vulnerable. The atmosphere is already changed, but the trajectory of future extremes remains, crucially, a matter of human decision.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of this passage?
options: To explain the scientific link between global warming and extreme weather and survey its consequences
To argue that individual weather events can never be studied scientifically
To compare the typical climates of several different continents
To promote one specific political policy as the only solution
questions.explanation: 全文先讲温室气体与升温的物理基础，再逐类分析热浪、干旱、暴雨、热带气旋，随后介绍归因科学、复合事件、不公平影响与适应/减缓对策，故 A 概括最全面。B 与原文的归因科学直接矛盾；C 并非比较各洲气候；D 原文主张减缓与适应结合，未推崇单一政策。

questions.question: According to the passage, roughly how much more water vapour can a warmer atmosphere hold per degree Celsius of warming?
options: 1 percent
3 percent
15 percent
7 percent
questions.explanation: 第5段引用 Clausius-Clapeyron 关系，指出温度每升高一摄氏度，大气可多容纳约百分之七的水汽，故 D 正确。其余数值均与原文给出的 7% 不符。

questions.question: What does the passage say about the field of attribution science?
options: It proves that every weather event is caused solely by climate change
It uses counterfactual modelling to estimate how much more likely or intense an event was made by climate change
It relies only on historical temperature records and rejects computer models
It is mainly used to predict the occurrence of earthquakes
questions.explanation: 第7段说明归因科学通过构建没有人为温室气体的'反事实'世界模型，比较事件概率或强度的变化，故 B 正确。A 错在 'solely'，原文明确说不是简单单一原因；C 错在它恰恰使用计算机模型；D 与地震无关。

questions.question: The word 'compound' as used in the passage (compound events) is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: simple
isolated
combined
temporary
questions.explanation: 第8段用 'compound events' 指热浪与干旱、暴雨与风暴等同时发生的组合，并强调其相互作用比单个灾害更严重，故词义为 'combined'（组合的），选 C。A 简单的、B 孤立的、D 暂时的均与文意相反。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the impacts of extreme weather from the passage?
options: They tend to fall hardest on populations with the fewest resources to prepare and recover
They are distributed equally across all regions and social groups
They affect only people living in coastal areas
They have been steadily declining in both frequency and severity
questions.explanation: 第9段指出贫穷国家、低收入社区、老人和户外劳动者风险更高，第10段又说保险退出高风险的社区难以重建，由此可推断资源最少者受害最重，故 A 正确。B 与 'profoundly unequal' 矛盾；C 忽略了内陆热浪与干旱；D 与全文趋势相反。

questions.question: Why does the author mention the 2003 European heatwave and the 2019-20 Australian fires?
options: To show that such events have now become impossible
To argue that these events were entirely natural in origin
To compare two different continents' insurance systems
To give concrete examples of extreme events linked to a warming climate
questions.explanation: 第3段以2003年欧洲热浪为例说明气候变暖使其发生概率翻倍，第4段以2019-20年澳大利亚山火说明火灾季变长变猛，二者都是为具体例证与变暖相关的极端事件，故 D 正确。A、B 与作者论述相反；C 文中未比较保险体系。

title: Beyond Fossil Fuels: The Global Transition to Renewable Energy
source: Adapted from energy policy and renewable technology publications
description: 全球可再生能源转型的技术、经济与政策
content:
The world's energy system is undergoing a transformation that is slow by the standards of marketing but rapid by the standards of infrastructure. For more than a century, coal, oil, and natural gas have supplied the overwhelming majority of commercial energy, powering industrial growth and raising living standards on a scale previously unknown. Yet the same combustion that delivered these benefits now accounts for the greater part of global greenhouse gas emissions, and it is increasingly recognized as both an environmental liability and a strategic vulnerability. In response, governments, companies, and households are investing in sources that draw on sunlight, wind, water, and heat from the Earth. The transition is already under way, but its pace, shape, and consequences vary enormously from one region to another.

The case for moving beyond fossil fuels rests on several arguments that reinforce one another. The environmental case is the most familiar: burning coal, oil, and gas releases carbon dioxide, the principal driver of climate change, along with pollutants that damage health. The economic case has strengthened as the cost of renewable technologies has collapsed. The security case matters too, because many countries depend on imported fuel from politically unstable regions, exposing themselves to price shocks and supply disruptions. There is also the argument of public health: the World Health Organization estimates that air pollution from burning fossil fuels contributes to millions of premature deaths each year. When these considerations are taken together, the transition begins to look less like an act of environmental virtue than a rational rearrangement of the energy system.

Solar photovoltaic technology illustrates the speed of change better than any other sector. In 2010, the cost of generating electricity from large-scale solar plants was several times that of conventional power. Today, in many markets, it is the cheapest source of electricity ever deployed. This dramatic decline has been driven by economies of scale in manufacturing, improvements in cell efficiency, and intense competition, particularly among Asian producers. The panels themselves have become more durable and easier to install, while software allows systems to be monitored remotely. Crucially, solar is modular: a utility can build a vast desert array, and a household can place panels on a roof, using the same basic technology. This flexibility has allowed solar to spread to places that never developed a conventional grid.

Wind power has followed a similar trajectory, though its physical logic is different. Modern turbines are extraordinary machines, with blades longer than a football pitch and towers that place the rotor high above turbulent ground-level air. Onshore wind is now competitive with fossil generation in many regions, while offshore wind, though more expensive to build and maintain, offers stronger and more consistent breezes. Offshore farms in the North Sea have demonstrated that very large projects can be delivered on schedule, and floating turbine designs promise to open deep-water sites that were previously inaccessible. A single large turbine can now generate enough electricity for thousands of homes, and the industry has developed sophisticated techniques for siting turbines to minimize their visual and ecological impact.

Other renewable sources fill important niches. Hydropower remains the largest source of renewable electricity worldwide, though its dependence on specific geography and its vulnerability to drought limit further expansion in many countries. Geothermal energy taps heat from beneath the Earth's surface and can provide a steady baseload supply, as in Iceland, where it heats most homes. Biomass can be burned for heat or converted into fuels, but its climate benefits depend critically on whether the vegetation is regrown, and poorly managed bioenergy can do more harm than good. Ocean energy, including tidal and wave devices, is still at an early stage but offers the advantage of predictability, since tides can be forecast with great accuracy.

Despite these advances, the defining technical challenge of a renewable-heavy system is variability. The sun does not shine at night, and the wind does not blow on demand. Electricity grids were designed around large dispatchable plants that could be ramped up or down to match consumption, and a rising share of variable generation requires a different approach. Planners now speak of the need for flexibility: the ability to balance supply and demand across time and space. This can be achieved in several ways, including geographically diverse generation so that a cloudy day in one region coincides with sun in another, expanded transmission lines to move power over long distances, and systems that can adjust consumption rather than only production.

Energy storage is the most visible part of this response. Lithium-ion batteries, whose price has fallen sharply alongside the growth of electric vehicles, can absorb surplus electricity during the day and release it during the evening peak. Grid-scale battery installations are now common in several countries, and they can respond to fluctuations within milliseconds, a speed that conventional plants cannot match. For longer-duration storage, pumped hydro remains the dominant technology, using surplus power to lift water uphill and releasing it through turbines when needed. Other options, such as flow batteries, compressed air storage, and the production of green hydrogen from water using renewable electricity, are being developed for applications where ordinary batteries are unsuitable. Each technology has its place, and most analysts expect a portfolio of solutions rather than a single winner.

The economics of the transition are changing as quickly as the technology. Analysts use a measure called the levelized cost of electricity, which compares the total lifetime cost of building and operating a plant with the amount of power it produces. On this basis, new solar and wind projects now undercut new coal plants in most parts of the world, even without subsidies. This has implications for developing countries, which can in principle leapfrog the fossil-intensive stage of development, just as many skipped fixed telephone lines in favour of mobile phones. However, the comparison is not straightforward: the cost of integrating variable generation into the grid, including storage and new transmission, must be added, and existing coal plants that have already been paid for can often operate cheaply in the short term.

Policy has therefore played a decisive role in shaping the pace of change. Early deployment was driven by feed-in tariffs and generous subsidies that guaranteed producers a price for their output, encouraging manufacturers to scale up and learn. As costs fell, many governments shifted to competitive auctions, in which companies bid to supply power at the lowest price, often driving costs down further. Carbon pricing, whether through taxes or emissions trading systems, improves the relative position of renewables by making pollution more expensive. Renewable portfolio standards require utilities to obtain a specified share of their power from clean sources. International agreements, notably the Paris Agreement, have created a framework of national commitments, though the strength of enforcement varies considerably.

The transition also faces material and social obstacles that are less often discussed. Batteries and turbines depend on minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and rare earth elements, whose extraction is concentrated in a handful of countries and can carry significant environmental and human-rights costs. Recycling these materials is technically possible but not yet widespread. Land use is another concern: utility-scale solar and wind farms require considerable space, and local opposition can delay projects for years. Grids in many regions are already congested, and connecting new generation can take longer than building it. Perhaps most sensitive is the question of employment, since communities that depend on coal mining or oil extraction face the loss of well-paid jobs, and a transition that ignores them risks generating political backlash.

These concerns have given rise to the idea of a just transition, which holds that the move to clean energy must be managed fairly. In practice this means investing in retraining and new industries in fossil-dependent regions, providing support for affected workers and their families, and ensuring that low-income households benefit from lower energy bills rather than bearing the costs. Energy access is a related priority: more than a billion people still lack reliable electricity, and for them the issue is not replacing fossil fuels but obtaining any modern supply at all. Off-grid solar systems are already transforming rural life in parts of Africa and Asia, powering lighting, refrigeration for medicines, and small businesses.

The direction of travel is now clear even though the route remains uncertain. Renewables have moved from a marginal niche to the centre of energy policy, and in many countries they are the default choice for new investment. The obstacles that remain are largely matters of infrastructure, finance, materials, and political will rather than fundamental scientific impossibility. Whether the transition proceeds quickly enough to limit climate change depends on decisions taken in the next decade about grid construction, storage deployment, mineral supply chains, and the protection of workers and consumers. The technologies are largely in place; the harder question is whether societies can organize themselves fast enough to use them.

questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The history of coal mining in industrial countries
Why fossil fuels can never be replaced by other sources
The technological, economic and policy dimensions of the global shift to renewable energy
The environmental impact of nuclear power generation
questions.explanation: 全文从技术（太阳能、风能、储能）、经济（成本下降、平准化电价）和政策（补贴、碳定价、国际协定）多角度论述全球能源转型，故 C 最全面。A 只涉及历史背景的一小部分；B 与全文主旨相反；D 文中几乎未讨论核电。

questions.question: According to the passage, what has happened to the cost of solar photovoltaic power over the past decade or so?
options: It has fallen dramatically, making solar competitive with fossil fuels in many markets
It has risen steadily because of shortages of raw materials
It has remained almost unchanged
It has fallen only in developing countries
questions.explanation: 第3段指出2010年大型太阳能发电成本是常规发电的数倍，如今在许多市场已成为最便宜的电力来源，故 A 正确。B、C 与原文的成本骤降矛盾；D 错在原文说这是全球性趋势，并非仅限发展中国家。

questions.question: Which of the following is mentioned as a way of managing the variability of wind and solar power?
options: Building more coal-fired power stations as a permanent backup
Banning the use of electricity during night-time hours
Reducing the number of wind farms in operation
Using battery storage, pumped hydro and demand response
questions.explanation: 第6段讲灵活性需求，第7段具体列举锂电池储能、抽水蓄能、需求侧调节及绿氢等方案，故 D 正确。A 与转型目标相悖；B 原文未提；C 恰恰相反。

questions.question: The word 'variability' as used in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: reliability
inconsistency
efficiency
affordability
questions.explanation: 文中 'variability' 指阳光和风力时有时无、不可按需供给的特性，即'不稳定性、波动性'，与 inconsistency 最接近，选 B。A 可靠性、C 效率、D 可负担性均不符合词义，且与后文需要灵活性来平衡供需的逻辑不符。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the renewable energy transition from the passage?
options: It will be completed everywhere within five years
It faces no significant economic or practical obstacles
It is technologically feasible but depends on policy, investment and supply chains

questions.question: What is the author's overall attitude toward the renewable energy transition?

Deeply pessimistic and dismissive of renewable technologies
Entirely neutral and purely descriptive, with no judgement
Hostile to any form of government intervention in energy markets

title: Thirsty Planet: The Growing Crisis of Water Scarcity
source: Adapted from water resources and environmental policy publications
description: 水资源短缺的成因、影响与管理策略
content:
Water appears to be the most abundant substance on Earth, covering more than seventy percent of the planet's surface. Yet this abundance is misleading, because the great majority of it is salty and therefore unusable for drinking or irrigation. Freshwater makes up only a small fraction of the total, and much of that is locked in glaciers and polar ice. The supply that humans can actually draw upon — rivers, lakes, and underground aquifers — is a tiny and finite share of the whole. As populations grow and patterns of consumption change, this limited resource is coming under pressure on every inhabited continent. The World Health Organization estimates that roughly two billion people lack safely managed drinking water, while a far larger number experience severe water scarcity for at least part of each year. The phrase 'thirsty planet' captures a paradox: there is enough water in the world in aggregate, but it is in the wrong places, at the wrong times, and increasingly in the wrong condition.

Water scarcity is usually divided into two types, though in practice they often overlap. Physical scarcity occurs when there is simply not enough water available to meet demand, as in arid regions where rainfall is low and unreliable. Economic scarcity occurs when water exists but people lack the infrastructure, money, or governance to access it safely. A city may sit beside a river and still suffer shortages if its pipes are broken, its treatment plants are inadequate, or its distribution network serves only the wealthy districts. This distinction matters because it changes the solution: physical scarcity calls for conservation, new sources, or reduced demand, while economic scarcity calls for investment, maintenance, and institutional reform. Many of the world's most acute crises are in fact a combination of the two.

The natural distribution of freshwater is strikingly uneven. Some regions, such as the Middle East and North Africa, receive little rainfall and rely heavily on groundwater or energy-intensive desalination. Others depend on seasonal monsoons that deliver most of the year's water in a few weeks, requiring enormous storage capacity to capture it. Major river systems such as the Nile, the Ganges, and the Yangtze support hundreds of millions of people but cross many political boundaries, making management a matter of diplomacy as much as engineering. Underground aquifers, which hold far more water than all rivers and lakes combined, have allowed cities and farming regions to flourish in places that would otherwise be uninhabitable. Yet these hidden reserves are being tapped far faster than they can naturally refill.

Human demand has risen dramatically, driven by population growth, urbanization, and changing diets. Global water withdrawals have increased many-fold over the past century, and agriculture accounts for roughly seventy percent of the total, mostly for irrigation. Producing a kilogram of grain requires hundreds of litres of water, and meat production requires considerably more because animals must be fed with crops first. As diets shift toward more meat in growing economies, the water embedded in food rises accordingly. Cities add their own pressures: concentrated populations need reliable supplies for drinking, sanitation, industry, and fire protection, while expanding urban areas seal the ground with concrete and reduce the amount of rainwater that can soak into the soil.

Climate change is now intensifying these pressures. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture and produces more erratic rainfall, so some regions face longer droughts while others experience heavier floods. The timing of water availability is changing: communities that rely on snowmelt may find that snow disappears earlier in the spring, leaving less water for the dry summer months. Glaciers that have served as natural reservoirs for generations are retreating, threatening the dry-season supply of large river systems. In coastal areas, rising sea levels push saltwater into freshwater aquifers, rendering wells unusable. These changes make historical rainfall records a less reliable guide for planning, since the assumptions behind dams, reservoirs, and irrigation systems may no longer hold.

The depletion of groundwater is among the most serious and least visible aspects of the crisis. In California's Central Valley, in the North China Plain, and beneath cities such as Delhi and Mexico City, water is being pumped from aquifers far faster than rainfall can replenish them. The consequences are dramatic: wells run dry, the land surface subsides as depleted sediments compact, and in coastal regions seawater intrudes inland. Unlike a lake, an aquifer may take centuries or even millennia to recover, so a decision to pump heavily today effectively consumes a resource that future generations will need. Because groundwater is hidden beneath the surface, its decline often goes unnoticed until the damage is advanced, and it is difficult to regulate where thousands of private wells are involved.

Pollution further reduces the usable supply. Industrial discharges, untreated sewage, and agricultural runoff carrying fertilizers and pesticides enter rivers and lakes, causing algal blooms that deplete oxygen and kill fish. Excess nitrogen and phosphorus, a process known as eutrophication, can turn a freshwater body into a green, toxic mass within a single season. Newer contaminants, including pharmaceuticals, microplastics, and persistent industrial chemicals, are increasingly detected in water supplies, and removing them is expensive. In many low-income countries, the absence of adequate sanitation means that water sources are contaminated with human waste, spreading cholera, dysentery, and other waterborne diseases. A river may therefore contain plenty of water while offering none of it in a form that is safe to drink.

The human consequences of scarcity are wide-ranging. Health suffers first, through dehydration, poor sanitation, and contaminated supplies. Food production becomes less reliable when irrigation water is rationed, raising prices and threatening livelihoods. Education is affected because children, and especially girls in many regions, may spend hours each day walking to fetch water, time that is lost from school. Economic activity slows when factories and farms cannot count on a steady supply, and unemployment can follow. Scarcity can also intensify social tensions: disputes between farmers and cities, between upstream and downstream regions, and between neighbouring countries sharing a river are becoming more common. Analysts sometimes describe water as a 'threat multiplier', a factor that worsens existing conflicts rather than causing them on its own.

Several episodes illustrate how quickly a seemingly secure supply can fail. Cape Town, a modern city of more than four million people, came close to 'Day Zero' in 2018, when taps were expected to be shut off after a sequence of dry winters; emergency restrictions and a sharp reduction in use averted the crisis, but only just. Chennai, on India's southern coast, faced a similar collapse of its reservoirs and groundwater. In the Colorado River basin, a prolonged drought and overallocation of water rights among seven American states and Mexico have forced difficult negotiations over how much each party must consume. These cases share a common lesson: even wealthy, well-governed cities can underestimate the fragility of their supplies, and infrastructure alone cannot protect against poor planning or prolonged drought.

Managing scarcity requires a combination of technical and institutional measures. Reducing leakage is often the cheapest option, since many municipal systems lose a substantial share of their water before it reaches a customer. Pricing reform can encourage conservation, though it must be designed carefully so that poor households are not punished for using what they need. In agriculture, drip irrigation and soil-moisture monitoring can deliver water directly to plant roots, greatly reducing waste compared with flood irrigation. Wastewater treatment and recycling allow water to be used several times, while desalination can provide a drought-proof supply for coastal cities, though at considerable financial and energy cost. No single measure is sufficient, and the most effective strategies combine several.

Governance is as important as technology. Water must be allocated among competing users — households, farmers, industry, and the environment — through rules that are seen as fair and are actually enforced. Because rivers and aquifers cross political boundaries, cooperation between regions and countries is essential, yet such agreements are difficult when one party believes it is receiving less than its share. Recognising these realities, rather than pretending they do not exist, is the first step toward reform. Investments in pipes and treatment plants will achieve little if the institutions responsible for maintaining them lack funding, transparency, or authority.

The outlook for water is serious but not hopeless. The past century demonstrated that engineering can supply cities and irrigate continents on an extraordinary scale; the challenge now is to do so without exhausting the resource base or worsening inequality. Climate change makes planning harder, but it also strengthens the case for using water more efficiently and protecting the ecosystems that regulate its flow. Ultimately, water scarcity is less a story of an empty planet than one of mismanagement and misplaced priorities. The technologies for recycling, conservation, and desalination already exist. What is often missing is the political will to price water honestly, maintain the infrastructure that delivers it, and treat access to a safe supply as a basic entitlement rather than a privilege.
