title: Editing Life: The Promise and Peril of Gene Editing
source: Adapted from bioscience and medical research publications
description: 基因编辑技术的医学前景与伦理争议
content:
In the span of a single decade, gene editing has moved from the edge of speculative biology to the centre of medical research and public debate. At its heart lies a deceptively simple idea: if the instructions of life are written in the chemical language of DNA, then it should be possible to find a faulty sentence and correct it. Tools such as CRISPR-Cas9 have made this possible with a precision and affordability that earlier generations of genetic engineering could only dream of. The implications are enormous. Conditions once considered untreatable might be cured at their source, crops could be made resilient to a changing climate, and entire species might be reshaped. Yet the same power that promises to relieve suffering also raises profound questions about safety, fairness, and the limits of human intervention in nature. This passage examines both the promise and the peril of a technology that is rewriting the book of life.

To understand why CRISPR has caused such excitement, it helps to understand how it works. The system was adapted from a natural defence mechanism used by bacteria to fight viruses. Scientists discovered that bacteria keep a record of viral DNA sequences and use a molecular scissor called Cas9, guided by a piece of RNA, to cut matching sequences when a virus returns. Researchers realised that they could replace the guide RNA with a custom-designed sequence that matches almost any gene in any organism. The guide leads Cas9 to the target, where it makes a clean cut in the DNA double helix. The cell then repairs the break, and in the process a new version of the gene can be inserted, disrupted, or corrected. Because designing a new guide is cheap and quick, CRISPR is far more accessible than earlier techniques such as recombinant DNA technology, which were laborious and expensive.

The most immediate applications are in medicine, where thousands of human diseases have a genetic component. Single-gene disorders, in which a mutation in one gene causes illness, are the most obvious targets. Sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, Huntington's disease, and certain forms of blindness all fall into this category. In 2019 and 2020, clinical trials reported promising results for patients with sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia, blood disorders affecting millions of people worldwide. Rather than editing the gene inside the body, doctors removed patients' stem cells, corrected the defect in the laboratory, and returned the cells after chemotherapy. Several patients became free of symptoms, a result that researchers described as a turning point in the treatment of inherited blood disease.

Beyond single-gene disorders, gene editing is being explored as a treatment for cancer, where it can be used to engineer immune cells to recognise and attack tumours. In a technique related to the well-known CAR-T therapy, a patient's T cells are modified so that they carry a receptor tuned to a specific cancer. Editing can also disable genes that allow a tumour to evade the immune system. Researchers are investigating treatments for infectious diseases too: one bold proposal uses gene drives to spread genes that make mosquitoes unable to transmit malaria, although this remains highly controversial. The reach of the technology therefore extends from rare inherited conditions to some of the biggest killers of our time.

Medicine is not the only field being transformed. In agriculture, gene editing offers a faster and more precise alternative to traditional breeding and to the older generation of genetically modified organisms. Because CRISPR can make small, targeted changes, it can, for example, switch off a gene that makes a plant susceptible to drought or disease without introducing foreign DNA. Scientists have developed mushrooms that resist browning, wheat with improved yield, and cattle that grow thicker coats in hot climates. Proponents argue that such innovations could help feed a growing population while reducing the environmental footprint of farming. Critics, however, warn that the long-term ecological effects are poorly understood and that the technology may concentrate power in the hands of a few large companies.

A crucial distinction in the ethics of gene editing is between somatic and germline modification. Somatic editing targets the cells of an existing patient, such as blood or liver cells. The changes affect only that individual and are not passed to children. Germline editing, by contrast, alters embryos, eggs, or sperm, so that the modification is inherited by every subsequent generation. This distinction is central to nearly every ethical debate. Somatic therapy is widely regarded as equivalent to other forms of medicine, provided it is safe and consented to. Germline editing, however, changes the human gene pool and affects people who cannot consent, namely future generations. For this reason it is treated with far greater caution by scientists and regulators alike.

The dangers of ignoring this distinction became clear in 2018, when a Chinese researcher named He Jiankui announced that he had used CRISPR to edit the embryos of twin girls, aiming to make them resistant to HIV. The announcement was met with almost universal condemnation. Scientists objected that the procedure was unnecessary, because simpler ways of preventing HIV transmission already existed, and that the edits were imprecise and potentially harmful. A subsequent investigation found that He had falsified records and ignored ethical oversight; he was eventually sentenced to prison. The episode demonstrated that scientific capability can race ahead of ethical consensus, and that a single irresponsible researcher can inflict lasting damage on public trust in an entire field.

Even in somatic therapy, safety remains a serious concern. The most widely discussed risk is the off-target effect: Cas9 may cut DNA at locations other than the intended one, especially if the guide RNA resembles several sequences in the genome. Such unintended cuts could disable a tumour-suppressing gene or activate one that causes cancer. Because the consequences may not appear for years, long-term monitoring of treated patients is essential. Researchers are developing more precise versions of the tool, including base editing, which changes individual DNA letters without making a double-strand break, and prime editing, a still newer technique often described as a genetic word processor. These refinements promise greater accuracy, but they also illustrate how quickly the field is evolving, often faster than the regulators who must assess it.

Beyond physical safety lie questions of fairness. Gene therapies developed so far are extraordinarily expensive; some treatments cost well over a million dollars per patient. This raises the prospect of a world in which the rich can afford genetic cures while the poor cannot, deepening existing inequalities. There is also the broader worry, often voiced under the phrase 'designer babies', that the technology could be used not to treat disease but to enhance traits such as intelligence, height, or appearance. Most scientists regard such uses as both unethical and scientifically premature, since these traits are influenced by many genes and by the environment. Nevertheless, the possibility forces societies to ask which interventions count as therapy and which cross a line into enhancement.

The regulatory response has been uneven. Many countries ban germline editing for reproductive purposes outright, while allowing somatic research under strict conditions. International conferences have issued statements calling for a moratorium on heritable human genome editing, but such declarations are not legally binding, and enforcement varies widely. The scientific community has begun to develop frameworks for responsible research, including registers of clinical trials and independent review boards. Yet a global problem arguably requires global rules. Critics argue that without an international body with real authority, a single irresponsible researcher in any country can undermine the trust on which the whole enterprise depends.

The story of gene editing is still being written, and it would be wrong to be either wholly optimistic or wholly fearful. The technology has already produced genuine medical benefits and could relieve suffering on a large scale. At the same time, its power to alter the inherited basis of life demands humility and careful oversight. The challenge is not to halt scientific inquiry but to guide it: to invest in safety, to ensure fair access, to distinguish medicine from enhancement, and to build institutions capable of judging new possibilities as they arise. If societies can meet that challenge, gene editing may come to be remembered as one of the great advances in human history. If they cannot, its promise may be overshadowed by preventable harm.

questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the central argument of the passage?
options: Gene editing has already been proven safe enough for unrestricted use in embryos
Gene editing offers major medical and agricultural benefits but demands careful ethical and safety oversight
The main obstacle to gene editing is a shortage of scientific ideas rather than regulation
Gene editing should be abandoned because its risks outweigh any possible benefit
questions.explanation: 全文先介绍 CRISPR 的原理与医学、农业应用，再用大量篇幅讨论体细胞与生殖细胞编辑的区分、脱靶风险、费用不公与监管问题，末段总结应'引导而非停止'研究，故主旨为 B。A 与原文相悖，作者明确强调安全性尚未解决；C 错，原文认为监管和伦理共识才是瓶颈；D 过于极端，作者并未主张放弃该技术。

questions.question: According to the passage, what distinguishes somatic editing from germline editing?
options: Somatic editing uses CRISPR while germline editing uses older recombinant methods
Somatic editing is always cheaper than germline editing
Somatic changes affect only the patient, whereas germline changes are inherited by future generations
Somatic editing is banned in most countries while germline editing is widely permitted
questions.explanation: 第6段明确指出体细胞编辑只影响患者本人、不会传给后代，而生殖细胞编辑改变胚胎或生殖细胞、会被后代继承，故选 C。A 错，两者都可用 CRISPR；B 原文未比较费用；D 恰好说反了，原文称许多国家禁止生殖细胞编辑用于生育目的。

questions.question: What is an 'off-target effect' as described in the passage?
options: Cas9 cutting DNA at unintended locations because the guide resembles several sequences
A patient developing immunity to the edited cells after treatment
The gradual loss of gene accuracy as a patient grows older
RNA guides being destroyed by the patient's immune system
questions.explanation: 第8段写道 'Cas9 may cut DNA at locations other than the intended one, especially if the guide RNA resembles several sequences in the genome'，即引导 RNA 相似导致误切，故选 A。B、D 所述免疫反应原文未提及；C 把脱靶误解为自然发生的基因退化，与原文所述酶切错误无关。

questions.question: The word 'moratorium' in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: A permanent financial reward
A detailed scientific explanation
A formal system of measurement
A temporary suspension of an activity
questions.explanation: 第10段提到国际会议呼吁对可遗传的人类基因组编辑实行 moratorium，结合语境及'不具法律约束力'可知是'暂停、暂缓'之意，故选 D。A、B、C 均与'暂停某项活动'的语义不符。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the case of He Jiankui from the passage?
options: His experiment was widely praised as a medical breakthrough
His work showed how individual actions can damage trust in an entire scientific field
He succeeded in producing HIV-resistant children with no ethical objections
His research was conducted with full international approval
questions.explanation: 第7段描述该事件遭到'几乎一致的谴责'，并指出一名不负责任的研究者会损害公众对整个领域的信任，故选 B。A、C 与'普遍谴责'相矛盾；D 错，原文明确说他伪造记录、无视伦理监督，并非获得国际批准。

questions.question: What is the author's overall attitude towards gene editing?
options: Complete rejection of all forms of genetic modification
Uncritical enthusiasm about its commercial potential
Cautiously supportive, emphasising both benefits and the need for oversight
Indifference, treating the debate as scientifically unimportant
questions.explanation: 作者既肯定'已带来真正的医学益处'，又强调安全、公平、区分治疗与增强以及制度建设，末段明确主张'不是停止而是引导'，故选 C。A 过于否定；B 忽视作者对伦理和风险的持续强调；D 与全文严肃讨论的语气明显不符。

title: The Driverless Revolution: Autonomous Vehicles on the Road Ahead
source: Adapted from transport technology and policy publications
description: 自动驾驶汽车的技术、监管与社会影响
content:
The motor car has been a defining technology of the modern age, but it may be undergoing its most radical transformation since the invention of the internal combustion engine. Autonomous vehicles, which can drive themselves without human input, have moved from science fiction to public roads in little more than a decade. Technology companies, traditional carmakers, and a host of startups are investing billions of dollars in the belief that the future of transport is self-driving. The stakes are high. Supporters predict fewer crashes, cleaner air, and a more accessible mobility system; sceptics point to unresolved technical problems, ethical dilemmas, and the loss of millions of jobs. This passage examines the technology, the promises, and the obstacles on the road ahead.

At the heart of an autonomous vehicle is a stack of sensors and software that replaces the human driver's eyes and judgement. Most systems combine cameras, which read road markings and traffic lights, with radar, which measures the speed of objects, and lidar, a laser-based sensor that builds a precise three-dimensional map of the surroundings. This data is fed into powerful onboard computers running machine-learning algorithms trained on millions of kilometres of driving. The vehicle uses the information to locate itself on a digital map, predict the behaviour of pedestrians and other cars, and decide when to accelerate, brake, or turn. Advances in computing power and in the quantity of training data have been central to recent progress.

Experts describe autonomy in levels, from zero, where the human does everything, to five, where the vehicle can drive anywhere in any conditions without human intervention. Most cars sold today sit at level two: they can maintain a lane or keep a distance from the car ahead, but the driver must remain attentive and ready to take over. Higher levels introduce difficult problems, because the handover between machine and human is a known weak point; a driver who has been watching a video may need several seconds to respond to a warning. This is why many companies have focused on restricted environments, such as motorways or city centres with detailed maps, rather than claiming full autonomy everywhere.

The strongest argument for self-driving cars is safety. Human error, including distraction, fatigue, and drunkenness, is estimated to cause more than ninety percent of road accidents. Machines do not drink, do not become sleepy, and can in principle react faster than a person. Proponents argue that if autonomous vehicles were to replace even a large fraction of human drivers, tens of thousands of lives could be saved each year. Companies such as Waymo have reported that their vehicles are involved in fewer crashes per kilometre than human-driven cars in the same areas. However, the data are not yet complete enough to prove the case, and a small number of high-profile accidents involving autonomous vehicles have raised awkward questions.

Beyond safety, autonomous vehicles could make transport more efficient. Because they can communicate with one another and with traffic infrastructure, they may be able to smooth the flow of traffic, reducing the stop-start patterns that waste fuel and increase congestion. In theory, platoons of vehicles could travel close together at high speed, cutting air resistance. There is also the possibility of robo-taxis: fleets of shared, driverless cars that could replace private ownership in cities. Since a private car is parked for the great majority of its life, shared autonomous vehicles could reduce the number of vehicles needed, freeing space currently devoted to parking.

The social benefits could be considerable for people who cannot drive. The elderly, the visually impaired, and those with mobility disabilities often depend on others for transport, which limits their independence and access to work, healthcare, and friends. Autonomous vehicles could give these groups the freedom to travel alone. They might also serve areas poorly covered by public transport, sometimes called transport deserts, where residents lack reliable connections to jobs and services. For planners, however, the question is whether the technology will be deployed in ways that help such communities or whether it will primarily benefit wealthy urban areas.

The transition will not be painless. Millions of people earn their living as professional drivers, including taxi drivers, bus drivers, and long-haul truckers. Automation could eliminate many of these jobs, and the disruption may be concentrated in particular regions and communities. Economists note that technological change usually destroys some jobs while creating others, but they also warn that the new positions may require different skills and may not appear in the same places. The political consequences of this shift are already visible in debates about the future of work. A serious policy response would include retraining and support for workers, rather than assuming the market will absorb the losses smoothly.

Regulators face an unusually difficult task. They must encourage innovation while protecting the public, and they must do so before the technology has fully settled. Rules that are too strict may drive development to less scrupulous jurisdictions; rules that are too loose may expose the public to untested vehicles. Different countries have taken different approaches, and even individual cities have imposed their own restrictions after incidents involving test vehicles. A particular problem is liability: if a self-driving car crashes, who is responsible, the passenger, the manufacturer, or the software developer? Until such questions are resolved, widespread deployment is likely to remain slow.

Autonomous vehicles also force societies to confront moral choices in a literal form. In an unavoidable collision, a human driver reacts instinctively, but a machine must be programmed with priorities. Should it swerve to avoid a child, even at the risk of harming its passengers? Should it value the lives of occupants above those of pedestrians? Studies in which members of the public are asked to make these trade-offs reveal wide disagreement across cultures. Philosophers warn that coding such decisions into vehicles is not a neutral technical exercise but an ethical one, and that the choices made by engineers will reflect particular values. Transparency about these decisions is therefore essential.

A further concern is cybersecurity. A vehicle that relies on software and wireless communication is potentially vulnerable to hacking. Researchers have demonstrated that connected cars can, in some circumstances, be remotely controlled, and the consequences of a malicious attack on a fleet of vehicles could be catastrophic. Manufacturers must therefore build robust defences and be prepared to issue security updates, much as they do for smartphones. There are also questions about data: self-driving cars will collect enormous amounts of information about where people go, and the handling of that data raises familiar issues of privacy.

Despite the difficulties, the direction of travel is clear. The technology is improving, trial fleets are expanding, and both industry and government are investing heavily. The most likely future is not an abrupt revolution but a gradual transition in which autonomous features spread from motorways to city streets, and from controlled conditions to more complex ones. How quickly this happens will depend less on engineering than on public trust, sensible regulation, and the ability of societies to manage the economic disruption. The driverless revolution may yet deliver its promised benefits, but only if its risks are confronted honestly rather than dismissed as teething problems.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of this passage?
options: To argue that autonomous cars should be banned from all public roads
To describe the technology and weigh its promised benefits against unresolved obstacles
To explain in detail how to program a self-driving car
To compare the cost of electric and petrol-powered vehicles
questions.explanation: 全文依次介绍传感器与算法、自动化级别、安全与效率收益、就业冲击、监管、伦理与安全风险，末段总结为渐进式过渡，目的在于全面评估利弊，故选 B。A 与末段的渐进乐观态度不符；C 只在第2段略述原理，并非全文目的；D 文中未做此类比较。

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the function of lidar in an autonomous vehicle?
options: It reads road markings and traffic lights
It measures the speed of nearby moving objects
It builds a precise three-dimensional map of the surroundings
It stores the vehicle's training data for later analysis
questions.explanation: 第2段写道 lidar 是 'a laser-based sensor that builds a precise three-dimensional map of the surroundings'，故选 C。A 是 cameras 的功能；B 是 radar 的功能；D 原文未提及，训练数据用于训练算法而非由激光雷达存储。

questions.question: Why does the passage describe the handover between machine and human as a weak point?
options: Because drivers who have been distracted may need several seconds to respond to a warning
Because human drivers always refuse to use lane-keeping technology
Because software cannot operate on motorways with detailed maps
Because cameras cannot detect road markings at high speed
questions.explanation: 第3段解释交接是薄弱环节，因为'看过视频的司机可能需要数秒才能对警告作出反应'，故选 A。B、D 原文无依据；C 恰好与原文相反，原文说许多公司正是在有详细地图的高速公路等受限环境测试。

questions.question: The phrase 'teething problems' in the final paragraph refers to which of the following?
options: Legal rules that apply exclusively to new drivers
Medical conditions affecting the teeth of passengers
Problems that can only be solved by young engineers
Early difficulties that are expected as a new technology develops
questions.explanation: 末段说风险不应'被当作初期小问题而置之不理'，结合语境可知 teething problems 指新技术发展初期不可避免的困难，故选 D。B 为字面误解；A、C 均脱离上下文，文中毫无依据。

questions.question: What can be inferred about robo-taxis from the passage?
options: They will certainly eliminate all private car ownership within a decade
They are already the most common form of transport in rural areas
They could reduce the number of vehicles needed and free up parking space
They are mainly intended to replace long-haul trucking
questions.explanation: 第5段指出私家车一生中大部分时间停着，共享无人驾驶车队可减少所需车辆数量、释放停车空间，故选 C。A'必然''十年内'过于绝对；B 与原文'主要惠及富裕城市地区'的疑虑不符；D 把 robo-taxi 与货运混淆。

questions.question: Which best describes the author's attitude towards the driverless revolution?
options: Fully convinced that benefits will arrive very soon
Cautiously optimistic, provided risks are managed honestly
Hostile because machines will never drive safely
Entirely neutral, with no indication of any expectation
questions.explanation: 作者承认技术改善、投资巨大，同时强调隐私、就业、监管等问题，末段说'若能诚实面对风险，无人驾驶革命仍可能带来承诺的益处'，故为谨慎乐观，选 B。A 忽略了诸多障碍；C 过于敌对；D 与作者明确的期待不符。

title: Powering the Future: The Race to Build Better Batteries
source: Adapted from energy technology and materials science publications
description: 电池技术进步与储能竞赛
content:
Modern life runs on batteries. They start our cars, power our phones, and increasingly store the electricity that lights our homes. For more than a century, the lithium-ion battery has been the dominant technology, quietly enabling the digital revolution. Yet as the world seeks to electrify transport and shift to renewable energy, the demands placed on batteries are growing far beyond what this technology was designed for. Governments and companies are now engaged in a global race to build cells that are cheaper, safer, longer-lasting, and made from materials that can be sourced responsibly. The outcome of this race will shape the pace of the energy transition.

To understand the challenge, it helps to understand how a lithium-ion battery works. A cell contains two electrodes, an anode and a cathode, separated by a liquid electrolyte. When the battery discharges, lithium ions move from the anode through the electrolyte to the cathode, while electrons flow through an external circuit, producing an electric current. Charging reverses the process. Lithium is ideal because it is light and highly reactive, which gives the battery a high energy density, meaning it stores a lot of energy for its weight. This is why lithium-ion batteries took over from older nickel-cadmium technology in portable electronics.

Despite its success, lithium-ion technology has limits that are becoming harder to ignore. Its energy density, though impressive by historical standards, is still far below that of petrol. This is why electric vehicles carry heavy battery packs and why range anxiety remains a barrier for many buyers. Charging speed is another constraint; even the fastest chargers take far longer than filling a fuel tank. The liquid electrolyte is flammable, which creates a risk of fires if a cell is damaged or overheated. Perhaps most importantly, the materials used, particularly lithium and cobalt, are finite and unevenly distributed, raising concerns about long-term supply.

Demand is growing at a remarkable rate. The International Energy Agency estimates that battery demand could rise by more than tenfold by 2030, driven mainly by electric vehicles and by grid storage. A single electric car may require a battery many times larger than that of a smartphone, and global sales of electric vehicles are expanding rapidly. At the same time, wind and solar power are intermittent: the sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow. Without large-scale storage, a grid rich in renewables would be unstable. Batteries are therefore becoming a central component of energy infrastructure, not merely a consumer accessory.

The scramble for raw materials has created both opportunities and problems. Lithium is concentrated in a handful of countries, with Australia and Chile among the largest producers, although demand has sent prices sharply higher. Cobalt, used in many cathodes, is mined largely in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where concerns about labour conditions and child labour have prompted criticism. Refining capacity is even more concentrated, with one country dominating the processing of several key materials. This concentration worries governments, which fear supply disruptions and price shocks similar to those affecting oil. In response, companies are seeking alternative chemistries and recycling strategies to reduce dependence on vulnerable supply chains.

The most closely watched contender is the solid-state battery. As the name suggests, it replaces the flammable liquid electrolyte with a solid material. This offers two advantages: it should be safer, because a solid is less likely to catch fire, and it may allow the use of a lithium metal anode, which could substantially increase energy density. Several major carmakers have invested heavily, and pilot production lines are operating. Yet solid-state cells face technical obstacles, including the tendency of tiny structures called dendrites to form and cause short circuits. Most experts believe they will appear in niche applications first and only later reach mass markets.

Other approaches are being pursued in parallel. Sodium-ion batteries use sodium, which is abundant and cheap, instead of lithium. They are likely to have lower energy density, but their low cost and plentiful materials make them attractive for stationary storage, where weight matters less. Flow batteries store energy in liquid tanks and can be discharged for many hours, which suits them to grid applications. Lithium iron phosphate cells, an older chemistry that avoids cobalt, have made a comeback because they are safer and less expensive, even though they store less energy per kilogram. The diversity of approaches reflects the fact that no single battery will suit every use.

As the first generation of electric vehicle batteries reaches the end of its life, recycling has moved up the agenda. A spent battery still contains valuable metals, and recovering them could reduce the need for mining while cutting costs. Today, however, only a small fraction of lithium-ion batteries are recycled, partly because collection is difficult and processes are expensive. New regulations in Europe and elsewhere require manufacturers to take responsibility for batteries at the end of their life, and several companies are building large recycling plants. If recycling becomes efficient at scale, it could transform the economics of battery materials and reduce environmental damage.

On the grid, the calculus is different. For stationary storage, cost per kilowatt-hour and lifespan matter more than weight, and here batteries are already competitive in many markets. Large installations built from thousands of cells can store surplus solar power during the day and release it in the evening, smoothing the matching of supply and demand. Such batteries can also respond almost instantly to fluctuations, helping to keep the grid stable in ways that traditional power stations cannot. Their deployment is growing faster than many forecasts predicted, and analysts see them as a key enabling technology for a low-carbon electricity system.

The economics of batteries have improved dramatically. The cost of a lithium-ion pack fell by roughly ninety percent between 2010 and 2020, as production scaled up and manufacturing improved. This decline, larger than most analysts had expected, has made electric vehicles increasingly competitive with petrol cars. Further reductions will be harder, because raw materials now account for a larger share of cost. Some observers argue that future progress will come as much from cleverer design and better manufacturing as from new chemistry. Others worry that a rush to secure materials could reverse the trend.

The race to build better batteries is therefore about more than a single invention. It is a contest involving chemistry, engineering, mining, manufacturing, and policy. No technology is likely to win outright, because different applications demand different properties: a phone, a car, and a power grid need quite different batteries. The most plausible future is a diversified landscape in which several chemistries coexist. What is clear is that better storage would accelerate the shift away from fossil fuels, and that the pace of that shift will depend, to a surprising degree, on how quickly the humble battery can be improved.

questions.question: What is the central theme of the passage?
options: Lithium-ion batteries will soon be replaced by a single superior technology
Improving batteries is a multi-front race essential to the energy transition
The main use of batteries is in portable electronics such as phones
Battery recycling has already solved the problem of raw material supply
questions.explanation: 全文从锂离子电池的局限讲到固态电池、钠离子、液流电池、回收与电网储能，末段明确指出没有单一技术会胜出、多种路线并存，且电池改进决定能源转型速度，故主旨为 B。A 与末段'多技术共存'相悖；C 只是背景，非中心；D 原文说回收比例仍很小，未解决问题。

questions.question: According to the passage, why are solid-state batteries considered safer?
options: They use sodium instead of lithium and cannot overheat
They replace the flammable liquid electrolyte with a solid material
They are recycled more easily than conventional cells
They are manufactured only for stationary grid storage
questions.explanation: 第6段指出固态电池 'replaces the flammable liquid electrolyte with a solid material'，固体不易着火因而更安全，故选 B。A 把钠离子电池的特点张冠李戴；C、D 原文均未作为固态电池安全性的原因。

questions.question: Which country is mentioned as the main source of cobalt, with associated labour concerns?
options: The Democratic Republic of Congo
Australia
Chile
China
questions.explanation: 第5段写道钴主要开采于 'the Democratic Republic of Congo'，并提到当地劳工条件与童工问题，故选 A。B、C 是锂的主要产地；D 在原文中是精炼产能集中的国家，并非钴矿来源。

questions.question: The word 'intermittent' in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: Constant and predictable
Extremely expensive to build
Irregular and not always available
Entirely free of carbon emissions
questions.explanation: 第4段解释 'the sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow'，说明风光发电是间歇性、不总可用的，故选 C。A 与原文相反；B、D 与 intermittent 一词的含义无关。

questions.question: What can be inferred about battery recycling from the passage?
options: It is already the cheapest way to obtain battery materials
It is unnecessary because raw materials are abundant everywhere
It is illegal in most European markets
It could become more important as new regulations force producers to take responsibility
questions.explanation: 第8段说目前回收比例很小，但欧洲等地新法规要求制造商承担报废电池责任、多家公司正建大型回收厂，由此可推断回收的重要性将上升，故选 D。A 原文未称其已最便宜；B 与关键材料稀缺、集中相矛盾；C 与原文'新法规要求回收'相反。

questions.question: What is the author's purpose in the final paragraph?
options: To prove that one chemistry will dominate all others
To argue that better storage, built through many approaches, will speed the shift from fossil fuels
To discourage further investment in battery research
To describe the history of the internal combustion engine
questions.explanation: 末段总结这是一场涉及化学、工程、采矿、制造与政策的竞赛，没有单一技术能通吃，多种电池将并存，而更好的储能会加速摆脱化石燃料，故选 B。A 与'没有单一技术胜出'直接矛盾；C、D 原文均无此意。

title: The Internet of Things: A Connected World and Its Discontents
source: Adapted from information technology and society publications
description: 物联网的普及、应用与隐私隐忧
content:
The internet began as a network of computers, then became a network of people, and is now becoming a network of objects. The Internet of Things, or IoT, refers to the billions of everyday devices that are equipped with sensors, software, and connectivity, allowing them to collect and exchange data. Thermostats, watches, refrigerators, traffic lights, and factory machines can all be part of this network. The idea is that connecting objects makes them smarter and more useful, enabling services that were previously impossible. Yet the same features that make the IoT powerful also make it intrusive and fragile. This passage explores how the connected world is being built, what it offers, and why it provokes unease.

The most visible examples are in the home. A smart thermostat learns a household's habits and adjusts heating accordingly, saving energy while keeping residents comfortable. Voice assistants can control lights, play music, and answer questions. Wearable devices such as fitness trackers monitor heart rate, sleep, and activity, encouraging users to take better care of their health. Refrigerators can report when food is running low, and washing machines can be started remotely. For many consumers, the appeal is convenience and a sense of control. For manufacturers, connected products open new revenue streams, since a device can be updated and serviced throughout its life.

The economic significance of the IoT is greatest in industry, where it is often called the Industrial Internet of Things. Factories fit machines with sensors that record temperature, vibration, and performance in real time. Engineers can then detect that a component is about to fail and replace it before production stops, a practice known as predictive maintenance. This can save considerable sums, because unplanned downtime is extremely costly. Logistics companies use connected sensors to track the location and condition of goods, from pharmaceuticals that must stay cool to containers crossing oceans. In agriculture, soil sensors tell farmers precisely when and where to irrigate, reducing waste.

In healthcare, connected devices are enabling a shift from hospital-centred care to continuous monitoring. Patients with chronic conditions can wear sensors that transmit data to their doctors, allowing problems to be spotted before they become emergencies. Implanted devices can adjust treatment automatically, and smart inhalers can record when a patient uses medication. During periods when face-to-face contact is difficult, such remote monitoring has proved especially valuable. The promise is a system that responds to actual health data rather than relying on occasional check-ups. However, the volume of personal information generated raises serious questions about who sees it and how it is protected.

At the urban scale, the IoT underpins many smart city ambitions. Traffic signals can adapt to real-time conditions, reducing congestion and emissions. Sensors can monitor air quality, detect leaks in water pipes, and report when public bins need emptying. Streetlights can dim when no one is around, cutting energy use. Planners hope that such systems will make cities more efficient and liveable. Yet critics note that a city filled with sensors is also a city in which movement and behaviour are constantly recorded, and that the benefits may not be evenly distributed between wealthy and poorer districts.

The case for the IoT rests on efficiency and insight. Data collected by connected devices can reveal patterns that were previously invisible, from the way a building uses energy to the early signs of a disease. Businesses can streamline operations, governments can allocate resources more effectively, and individuals can make better-informed choices. In principle, the IoT allows the physical world to be managed with the same precision that software brings to the digital world. Estimates of the economic value at stake run into trillions of dollars, which explains the enthusiasm of investors and the urgency of governments.

The central objection concerns privacy. Every connected device creates data, and data about a person's home, health, or movements can be intensely revealing. Consumers often do not understand what is collected or how long it is kept, and the terms of service governing devices are rarely read. Data can be combined from multiple sources to build detailed profiles, then used for advertising or sold to third parties. In many jurisdictions, laws written before the rise of the IoT offer weak protection. Privacy advocates argue that consent obtained through a long, unread document is not real consent, and that the burden should shift towards collecting less data in the first place.

Security is an equally serious problem. Many IoT devices are designed cheaply, with little attention to updates or passwords, and once installed they may remain in service for years. This makes them attractive targets. In a famous incident, a network of compromised cameras and other devices was used to launch a massive denial-of-service attack that disrupted websites across the world. Hackers have shown that they can sometimes control connected cars and medical devices, raising the possibility of physical harm. Unlike a computer, a device with a security flaw cannot simply be patched if the manufacturer has stopped supporting it.

A more practical obstacle is fragmentation. Devices from different manufacturers often use different standards and cannot easily communicate with one another. A smart lock may not work with a smart home hub from another company, and the data from one health app may not be readable by another system. This limits the usefulness of the technology and frustrates users. Industry bodies have attempted to agree common standards, but progress is slow because companies have commercial reasons to prefer their own systems. Regulators are increasingly interested in requiring interoperability, much as earlier generations of rules opened up telecommunications networks.

There is also a risk that the IoT will deepen existing inequalities. Many benefits flow to those who can afford connected devices and have reliable internet access, while others are left with older, less efficient technology. In poorer countries, the cost of connectivity and the lack of infrastructure may limit adoption, creating a further gap. Within wealthy societies, the elderly and less technically confident may struggle to use devices that assume digital literacy. If the connected world is to be genuinely inclusive, attention must be paid to affordability, design, and access, not simply to the speed of innovation.

The Internet of Things is not a passing fashion but a continuing expansion of computing into the physical world. Its potential to improve health, efficiency, and daily life is real, and many useful applications are already in place. But the discontents are also real: privacy erosion, weak security, incompatible systems, and unequal access. The question is not whether to embrace the technology but how to govern it. Stronger standards, clearer rules about data, and devices designed with security in mind would help. If these measures are adopted, the connected world could deliver broad benefits; if not, its growth may outpace the safeguards that make it trustworthy.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The IoT offers useful applications but raises serious privacy, security and equity concerns that require governance
The IoT is a passing fashion that will soon disappear
Smart home devices are the only meaningful application of the IoT
Privacy laws have already fully solved the problems created by connected devices
questions.explanation: 全文先讲物联网在家庭、工业、医疗、城市的应用与效益，再用多段讨论隐私、安全、标准碎片化和数字鸿沟，末段提出核心是'如何治理'，故选 A。B 与末段'并非昙花一现'矛盾；C 缩小了范围，工业应用才是经济意义最大之处；D 原文说法规保护仍然薄弱。

questions.question: What is predictive maintenance as described in the passage?
options: Replacing all factory machines at fixed intervals
Using sensors to detect a failing component before production stops
Predicting which products consumers will buy next year
Scheduling maintenance only after a breakdown has occurred
questions.explanation: 第3段说明传感器实时记录机器状况，工程师可在部件即将失效时、停产之前更换，即预测性维护，故选 B。A 是定期更换，非按状态预测；C 与维护无关；D 恰好与'在故障前更换'相反。

questions.question: According to the passage, what happened in the famous incident involving connected devices?
options: They were used to monitor patients' heart rates
They were recalled because they consumed too much energy
A network of cameras and other devices was used to launch a massive denial-of-service attack
They were hacked to change the price of household electricity
questions.explanation: 第8段提到一起著名事件：被攻破的摄像头等设备网络被用于发起大规模拒绝服务攻击、扰乱网站，故选 C。A、D 原文无此事；B 把能耗问题与网络攻击混为一谈。

questions.question: The word 'fragmentation' in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: Rapid growth in the number of devices
Division into incompatible systems and standards
A sudden failure of computer security
The process of collecting personal data
questions.explanation: 第9段解释不同厂商设备使用不同标准、无法互相通信，故 fragmentation 指 fragmented、互不兼容的碎片化状态，选 B。A 是 proliferation 的含义；C、D 与本段主题无关。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the author's view of data consent?
options: Consent given through long unread terms is genuine and sufficient
Consent should be replaced by a ban on all data collection
Consumers already understand exactly how their data is used
Meaningful consent would require collecting less data and clearer information
questions.explanation: 第7段指出通过冗长未读文件获得的同意并非真正的同意，负担应转向少收集数据，故可推断作者认为真正同意需要更少的数据收集和更清晰的信息，选 D。A 与作者明确观点相反；B 过于极端；C 与'消费者常不了解'相矛盾。

questions.question: What is the author's main purpose in writing this passage?
options: To encourage people to buy more smart devices
To argue for thoughtful governance so that the connected world can deliver broad benefits
To prove that the IoT has no practical value
To describe the technical design of a particular smart home hub
questions.explanation: 末段明确说问题不在于是否拥抱技术而在于如何治理，并建议更强标准、更清晰的数据规则和注重安全的设计，故选 B。A 与作者的审慎态度不符；C 与前文列举的诸多效益矛盾；D 文中并未具体描述某产品设计。

title: The New Space Age: Commercialization Beyond Earth
source: Adapted from space exploration and aerospace industry publications
description: 商业航天兴起与太空探索新格局
content:
For most of the twentieth century, space exploration was the preserve of governments. It was an arena of national prestige, conducted by agencies such as NASA and its counterparts, and justified by scientific discovery and Cold War rivalry. That era is giving way to something quite different. A new space age is taking shape, led not only by states but by private companies with ambitious commercial goals. Rockets that once cost hundreds of millions of dollars are being reused, satellites are being launched in their thousands, and tourists are paying for journeys to the edge of space. This passage examines the forces driving the commercialisation of space and the opportunities and risks that follow.

The single most important change has been the arrival of reusable rockets. Traditionally, launch vehicles were discarded after a single use, which made access to orbit extraordinarily expensive. Companies such as SpaceX developed boosters that return to Earth and land vertically, ready to be flown again. Reusing a rocket does not eliminate all costs, because refurbishment and fuel are still required, but it has reduced the price of placing a kilogram into orbit by a large margin. Competitors, including established aerospace firms, have followed suit. Falling launch costs are the foundation on which nearly every other commercial space activity depends.

The most visible consequence is the proliferation of satellites. A single launch can now place dozens of small satellites into orbit, and companies plan constellations of thousands. These can provide internet access to remote regions, improve navigation, monitor crops, and track ships and aircraft. Earth observation satellites are producing images with increasing resolution and frequency, useful for everything from disaster response to verifying environmental agreements. The result is a space economy in which data, rather than merely exploration, generates revenue. Some analysts believe that the market for space-based services will grow to be worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

Governments have increasingly chosen to purchase services from private firms rather than own and operate every system themselves. Cargo and crew flights to the International Space Station are now routinely supplied by commercial vehicles, and several companies have developed their own spacecraft. This shift, sometimes described as a new division of labour between public and private sectors, aims to cut costs and encourage innovation. Supporters argue that competition has produced faster progress than traditional procurement. Critics counter that relying on a handful of companies creates risk, and that the public interest may not always align with commercial incentives.

The ambitions extend far beyond low Earth orbit. Several nations and private ventures are planning a return to the Moon, with the stated aim of establishing a permanent presence. Further ahead, the colonisation of Mars is discussed with growing seriousness, although the technical obstacles are formidable. A crewed mission to Mars would take many months, expose astronauts to radiation and muscle loss, and require the production of fuel and food on arrival. Advocates see such projects as the next great chapter of human exploration; sceptics regard them as expensive distractions from problems on Earth. Either way, they are driving investment in life-support systems and robotics.

Space tourism has moved from fantasy to a small but real industry. Suborbital flights carry passengers a few minutes above the atmosphere, offering a brief experience of weightlessness and a view of the curvature of the Earth. These flights are currently expensive, available only to the wealthy, and carry environmental questions about their emissions. Longer stays in orbit are offered by a few companies, and dedicated space stations are being designed. Observers are divided: some see tourism as a legitimate source of revenue that will help fund larger ambitions, while others regard it as conspicuous consumption of resources at a time of climate concern.

As activity increases, so does the problem of space debris. Orbit is littered with defunct satellites, spent rocket stages, and fragments from collisions, all travelling at enormous speed. Even a small piece of debris can destroy a functioning satellite, creating more fragments in a cascade sometimes described as the Kessler syndrome. Several constellations of thousands of satellites have raised alarm among astronomers, whose observations are affected by bright objects crossing the sky, and among regulators concerned about collision risks. Engineers are developing systems to remove debris and to ensure that satellites can be deorbited safely at the end of their lives.

The legal framework governing space has not kept pace with technology. The foundational treaty of 1967 assigns responsibility for space activities to nations, even when the actors are private companies, and prohibits national claims of sovereignty over celestial bodies. This creates awkward questions: who licenses a private mission to the Moon, and who is liable if it causes damage? Some countries have passed national laws to authorise and supervise their companies, but standards differ. Without greater international coordination, there is a risk of conflicting rules and a race to the bottom in safety and environmental protection.

A more contentious prospect is the extraction of resources from the Moon or asteroids. Water ice at the lunar poles could be turned into drinking water and rocket fuel, and some asteroids contain valuable metals. Advocates argue that using local resources would make deep-space missions far more practical, since launching everything from Earth is prohibitively expensive. Opponents warn of a new scramble for territory, in which wealthy nations and corporations claim the most valuable sites. The legal position on owning resources extracted from space is unsettled, and the issue is likely to become a major diplomatic challenge in the years ahead.

The new space age is also reshaping geopolitical competition. More countries now possess launch capability, and space is increasingly intertwined with national security through satellites used for communication, navigation, and surveillance. The same technologies that serve civilian purposes can support military ones, and the boundary between the two is often blurred. Some analysts speak of a NewSpace era in which the growing number of actors makes conflict both more likely and harder to manage. Establishing norms of behaviour in orbit has therefore become an urgent diplomatic task, even as the economic opportunities expand.

The commercialisation of space is neither wholly a threat nor an unqualified triumph. It has already lowered costs, accelerated innovation, and opened possibilities that seemed remote a generation ago. At the same time it creates genuine risks, from orbital congestion to unequal access and contested resources. The challenge for the coming decades is to build institutions capable of managing shared spaces before the pressures become acute. If governance keeps pace with enterprise, the new space age could bring benefits that extend well beyond the spacefaring nations. If it does not, the promise of expansion may be overshadowed by avoidable conflict and damage.

questions.question: What is the main argument of this passage?
options: Space exploration should be returned entirely to government control
Commercial space activity brings innovation and opportunity but needs stronger governance to manage its risks
Space tourism is the only commercially viable space activity
International space law is already adequate for the new era
questions.explanation: 全文既肯定可复用火箭、卫星服务、旅游创新带来成本下降与新机遇，又用多段讨论太空垃圾、法律滞后、资源争夺与地缘风险，末段强调需建立治理机制，故主旨为 B。A 与全文对商业创新的肯定不符；C 缩小范围，文中谈及多种商业活动；D 原文明确说法律框架已跟不上技术。

questions.question: According to the passage, what has been the single most important change in space activity?
options: The arrival of reusable rockets that lower the cost of reaching orbit
The discovery of water ice on the Moon
The construction of new space stations
The signing of the 1967 treaty
questions.explanation: 第2段开头明确指出最重要的变化是可复用火箭的出现，它大幅降低了进入轨道的成本，故选 A。B、C 是后文提到的后续发展；D 是 1967 年既有条约，并非新变化。

questions.question: What is the Kessler syndrome as mentioned in the passage?
options: A method for removing space debris safely
A treaty governing the use of celestial bodies
A cascade of collisions creating increasing amounts of orbital debris
A technique for landing rockets vertically
questions.explanation: 第7段说明小碎片可摧毁卫星并产生更多碎片，形成被称作 Kessler syndrome 的连锁效应，故选 C。A 是应对措施而非该现象；B 是法律概念；D 是火箭回收技术，均不符。

questions.question: The word 'proliferation' in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: Rapid increase
Careful control
Sudden disappearance
Official examination
questions.explanation: 第3段说最明显的后果是卫星的 proliferation，接着解释一次可发射数十颗、计划组建数千颗的星座，可知意为'激增、扩散'，故选 A。B、C、D 均与数量激增的语境不符。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the 1967 treaty from the passage?
options: It explicitly authorises private companies to mine asteroids
It has been replaced by a newer international agreement
It was written before private companies became major space actors and leaves gaps
It assigns liability solely to individual astronauts
questions.explanation: 第8段指出 1967 年条约把责任分配给国家、禁止主权声明，但当时私人公司并非主要行为者，由此产生许可与责任等尴尬问题，可推断该条约存在空白，故选 C。A 原文未说条约授权采矿；B 未被取代；D 说责任仅归宇航员个人，与'责任归于国家'相反。

questions.question: Which best describes the author's attitude towards the commercialisation of space?
options: Indifferent to the economic and political changes described
Entirely negative about all private space ventures
Unconditionally celebratory with no reservations
Balanced: acknowledging progress while urging caution and coordination
questions.explanation: 末段称商业化'既非纯粹威胁也非完全胜利'，既肯定降本创新，又提醒轨道拥堵、资源争夺等风险并呼吁治理，故为平衡审慎的态度，选 D。B、C 均过于极端；A 与作者明显关注这些变化不符。

title: Generating Change: How Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Medicine
source: Adapted from medical technology and healthcare research publications
description: AI在诊断、药物研发与个性化医疗中的应用
content:
Artificial intelligence has moved from the research laboratory into the clinic. Algorithms now assist doctors in interpreting scans, help chemists search for new drugs, and tailor treatments to the genetic makeup of individual patients. This shift is often described as a revolution in medicine, and the scale of investment suggests that many people take the claim seriously. Yet the reality is more complex than the headlines. AI can perform some tasks better than humans, but it can also fail in ways that are difficult to predict. This passage examines where the technology is making a difference, what limits it, and how medicine is adapting.

The most mature application is medical imaging. Machine-learning systems can be trained on large collections of X-rays, CT scans, and MRI images to spot patterns associated with disease. In some studies, algorithms have matched or exceeded the accuracy of experienced radiologists in detecting conditions such as diabetic retinopathy, certain cancers, and pneumonia. A system can examine an image in seconds, flagging suspicious areas for a doctor to review. This does not make radiologists redundant; rather, it can reduce fatigue and help them focus on difficult cases. Here AI functions as a tireless assistant rather than a replacement.

Developing a new drug is famously slow and expensive, often taking more than a decade and costing billions of dollars. AI is being used to shorten several stages of this process. Algorithms can analyse vast chemical libraries and predict which molecules are likely to bind to a target associated with a disease, narrowing the search before expensive laboratory work begins. During the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, AI models helped identify potential compounds and predict how the virus might evolve. Several companies now use AI to design molecules from scratch. The hope is not that AI eliminates experiments, but that it makes each experiment more likely to succeed.

Perhaps the most far-reaching change is in personalised, or precision, medicine. Every person's genetic makeup, lifestyle, and environment differ, and the same drug may work well for one patient and poorly for another. AI can combine genetic data, medical history, and information from wearable devices to estimate which treatment is most likely to help a particular individual. In cancer care, algorithms already help match patients to therapies based on the mutations in their tumours. Results that once required years of trial and error may eventually be predicted in advance, sparing patients ineffective treatments and reducing costs.

Related to personalisation is predictive analytics. By analysing the records of many patients, models can identify those at high risk of developing a condition such as heart failure or sepsis, sometimes days before symptoms become obvious. Hospitals have begun to use such systems to intervene earlier, for example by monitoring high-risk patients more closely. Prediction can also support discharge planning: an algorithm may flag a patient likely to be readmitted, allowing staff to arrange follow-up support. These applications illustrate a broader shift from reacting to illness towards anticipating it.

Despite the optimism, significant obstacles remain. An AI system learns from the data it is given, and medical data are often incomplete, inconsistent, or biased. A model trained mainly on patients from one country or ethnic group may perform poorly on others, potentially worsening health inequalities. Algorithms can also pick up misleading shortcuts: a system might learn to detect a disease from the type of scanner used rather than from the disease itself. When the model is moved to a different hospital, it then fails. Researchers refer to this problem as poor generalisability, and it is one of the main reasons why promising results in research do not always survive in practice.

A further difficulty is the so-called black box problem. Many powerful models, particularly deep neural networks, produce answers without revealing how they reached them. In medicine, where a decision may have serious consequences, doctors and patients want to understand the reasoning. If an algorithm recommends a treatment, the clinician needs to know which features influenced the recommendation. This has led to a field of research known as explainable AI, which seeks to make models more transparent. Regulators are also beginning to require explanations for certain automated decisions. Without trust and understanding, even accurate systems may be rejected by the people who must use them.

Regulation is struggling to keep pace. A conventional drug is tested in carefully designed trials, but an algorithm may change as it is updated with new data. This makes it hard to apply traditional approval processes, which assume a fixed product. Agencies have begun to develop new frameworks for software as a medical device, yet the rules vary between countries and continue to evolve. There is also the question of liability: if an AI system gives a wrong recommendation, is the fault with the doctor, the hospital, or the company that wrote the software? These unresolved questions create uncertainty for both developers and clinicians.

The ethical questions are equally substantial. Patient consent is complicated when an algorithm uses personal health records to train a commercial product. There are concerns about privacy, since the data involved are among the most sensitive that exist. Some commentators worry about automation bias, the tendency of clinicians to trust a machine's answer too readily, especially under pressure. Others point to the risk that responsibility becomes diffuse, with no single person clearly accountable for an outcome. Addressing these issues requires not only technical safeguards but also clear professional guidelines and honest discussion with patients about the role of machines in their care.

For all these reasons, the most persuasive vision is one of collaboration rather than substitution. AI is good at processing enormous quantities of data, spotting subtle patterns, and working without fatigue. Humans remain better at exercising judgement, understanding context, and communicating with patients. The most effective clinical systems combine the two: algorithms handle routine analysis, while doctors interpret results in the light of the whole person. Studies suggest that such partnerships can outperform either alone. The question for the coming years is how to design workflows and training that make the partnership work in practice.

The transformation of medicine by AI is real but uneven. Some applications, especially in imaging, are already established; others, such as fully personalised treatment, remain aspirational. The technology's limits are as important as its capabilities, because medicine demands not only accuracy but also reliability, transparency, and trust. If developers, regulators, and clinicians can address the weaknesses, AI could help deliver better care to more people at lower cost. If they cannot, the risk is that early enthusiasm gives way to disappointment, and that potentially useful tools are abandoned because the conditions for their success were never created.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?
options: AI will completely replace doctors within the next few years
AI is transforming medicine in several areas but faces technical, ethical and regulatory limits
AI is used mainly to reduce the cost of hospital buildings
Medical imaging is the only area where AI has any application

questions.question: According to the passage, how is AI currently used in medical imaging?

It trains medical students through virtual simulations

questions.question: What does the passage identify as 'poor generalisability'?
options: A model performing poorly when applied to a different hospital or population
The inability of algorithms to process large images
A patient's refusal to share medical data

No longer considered useful

questions.question: What can be inferred about regulating medical AI from the passage?

Because algorithms change with new data, traditional fixed-product approval is hard to apply

questions.question: Which best describes the author's attitude towards AI in medicine?
options: Enthusiastic and entirely uncritical
Cautiously positive, favouring collaboration between AI and clinicians
Hostile, viewing AI as a threat to patient safety
Convinced that personalised medicine will never be possible

title: Robots on the Line: Automation and the Future of Manufacturing
source: Adapted from industrial technology and economics publications
description: 制造业自动化升级及其经济社会影响
content:
The factory has always been a place where machines replace human effort. From the mechanical loom to the assembly line, each generation of technology has changed what workers do and how they do it. Today, a new wave of automation is reshaping manufacturing once again. Robots have become cheaper, more flexible, and more intelligent, and they are spreading beyond the huge plants of the car industry into smaller workshops. Supporters see higher productivity, better quality, and safer workplaces. Critics worry about lost jobs and the concentration of wealth. This passage examines the changes under way and their economic and social consequences.

Manufacturing robots come in several forms. The familiar industrial arm, often bolted to the floor, performs repetitive tasks such as welding, painting, and lifting with great speed and precision. These machines are typically programmed to repeat one motion exactly. A newer category, known as collaborative robots or cobots, is designed to work alongside people. Cobots are smaller, slower, and equipped with sensors that stop them when they come near a human, making them safer for shared workspaces. Advances in vision systems and grippers allow robots to handle objects that vary in shape and position, tasks that were once beyond them.

The economic case for robots is straightforward. They can work continuously without breaks, maintain consistent quality, and operate in conditions that are dangerous or uncomfortable for people, such as high temperatures or exposure to fumes. In the automotive industry, a single plant may use hundreds of robots, and the precision they bring has made modern vehicles more reliable. Electronics manufacturers rely on robots for assembling tiny components that would be difficult for human hands. Because robots can be reprogrammed, they also allow manufacturers to change products more quickly, an advantage in markets where consumer preferences shift fast.

The current wave is distinguished by connectivity. In what is often called Industry 4.0, machines are linked to networks and exchange data in real time. A factory can monitor the condition of every robot, predict maintenance needs, and adjust production automatically when demand changes. Sensors collect information that is analysed to reduce waste and improve efficiency. Digital models of the entire production line, sometimes called digital twins, allow managers to test changes before making them physically. The result is a more responsive and integrated system, in which the boundary between the physical and digital sides of manufacturing becomes blurred.

The effect on employment is the most contested issue. Robots clearly displace workers in tasks that are repetitive and predictable. Studies that attempt to quantify the effect often conclude that a significant share of manufacturing jobs is at risk, particularly those involving routine manual work. Unlike earlier waves of automation, which mainly affected manual labour, new systems based on artificial intelligence can also perform some cognitive tasks, such as inspection and basic decision-making. This has led to anxiety that the change will be broader and faster than previous transitions, giving workers and communities less time to adapt.

Yet the picture is not simply one of loss. Automation creates jobs as well as removing them: robots must be designed, installed, programmed, maintained, and supervised. Demand grows for technicians, engineers, and data analysts. Higher productivity can lower prices and increase output, which may support employment elsewhere in the economy. Historically, fears that machines would cause permanent mass unemployment have not been realised, because new industries and occupations have emerged. However, economists caution that this time the transition may be uneven, with gains concentrated in particular regions and skills, while the losses fall on workers who cannot easily retrain.

An important change is that automation is becoming accessible to smaller companies. Until recently, industrial robots were expensive and required specialist integration, putting them beyond the reach of small and medium-sized manufacturers. Falling prices, simpler programming, and the growth of cobots have lowered the barrier. Small firms can now automate a single task without rebuilding a whole production line. This could help them compete with larger rivals and bring some manufacturing back to countries where labour costs are high. Policymakers see potential in this trend, since a revived base of small manufacturers can support resilient local economies.

There is, however, a risk that the benefits will be concentrated. The firms that design and own the most advanced systems may capture a disproportionate share of the gains, while the factories that merely use them face high costs and dependence on a few suppliers. Some observers describe a winner-takes-most dynamic, in which a handful of large companies dominate global production. The geographic distribution of manufacturing may also change, as companies locate production close to markets and skilled workers rather than wherever labour is cheapest. These shifts have implications for trade, urban economies, and the livelihoods of communities built around traditional industry.

The challenge for workers is essentially one of skills. As routine tasks are automated, the tasks that remain tend to require problem-solving, adaptability, and technical knowledge. Workers who can operate, maintain, and improve automated systems are in demand, while those whose jobs consist of repetition face the greatest risk. This has put pressure on education and training systems to respond more quickly. Many companies have begun to invest in retraining their own staff, recognising that skills shortages can hold back adoption. Governments, for their part, are exploring ways to support lifelong learning, though results to date are mixed.

Looking ahead, the integration of artificial intelligence and robotics is likely to accelerate the trend. Robots that can learn from demonstration, recognise objects reliably, and adapt to new tasks will be able to work in environments that are currently too variable for automation, such as warehouses, farms, and construction sites. Some analysts expect a shift from mass production toward more customised output, since flexible robots can switch between products easily. The factory of the future may therefore employ fewer people than its predecessor, but those people will need broader skills and will work alongside machines as colleagues rather than merely as operators.

Automation in manufacturing is neither a simple story of destruction nor one of effortless progress. It offers real gains in productivity, quality, and safety, and it can support new industries and better jobs. At the same time it disrupts established communities and concentrates opportunities in ways that markets alone will not correct. The outcome will depend on choices: how training is provided, how the gains are shared, and how quickly institutions adapt. If societies manage the transition well, automation could raise living standards and make work safer. If they do not, the technology may deepen divisions that its supporters now overlook.

questions.question: What is the central argument of this passage?
options: Automation offers real benefits but its disruptive effects require thoughtful management
Robots have no place in modern manufacturing
Only large car factories can afford to automate
Automation will certainly create more jobs than it destroys in every region
questions.explanation: 全文既论述生产力、质量、安全等收益，又讨论就业冲击、利益集中与技能挑战，末段强调结果取决于培训与收益分配等选择，故主旨为 A。B 与全文对自动化的肯定矛盾；C 与第7段小企业也能采用相悖；D'必然''每个地区'过于绝对。

questions.question: What feature makes collaborative robots safer to work alongside humans?
options: They are programmed to repeat one motion exactly
They have sensors that stop them when near a person
They are bolted firmly to the factory floor
They operate only at very high temperatures
questions.explanation: 第2段说协作机器人更小、更慢，并装有传感器，靠近人时会停下，从而在共享空间更安全，故选 B。A 是传统工业机械臂的特点；C 恰恰是传统机械臂的安装方式；D 与原文'避免危险环境'无关。

questions.question: According to the passage, what does 'Industry 4.0' emphasise?
options: Connecting machines to networks and exchanging data in real time
Returning manufacturing to hand tools
Eliminating all human workers from factories
Producing only customised goods for wealthy buyers
questions.explanation: 第4段说明 Industry 4.0 的特点是机器联网、实时交换数据，从而监控状态、预测维护、用数字孪生测试改动，故选 A。B 与自动化方向相反；C 原文未说完全消除工人；D 只是未来可能趋势之一，并非 Industry 4.0 的定义。

questions.question: The word 'displace' in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: To promote someone to a higher position
To provide new training for a worker
To take over someone's job or force them out of work
To measure the output of a machine
questions.explanation: 第5段说机器人在重复性和可预测任务上'clearly displace workers'，即取代工人、使其失业，故选 C。A、B、D 均非 displace 在文中的含义。

questions.question: What can be inferred about small manufacturers from the passage?
options: They will certainly be driven out of business by large firms
Falling robot prices and cobots make automation increasingly reachable for them
They refuse to adopt any new technology
They mainly produce goods for the aerospace industry
questions.explanation: 第7段指出价格下降、编程简化和协作机器人的出现降低了门槛，小企业可只自动化一道工序，故可推断 B 正确。A 与原文'帮助小企业竞争'矛盾；C、D 文中无依据。

questions.question: What is the author's purpose in the final paragraph?
options: To describe the invention of the mechanical loom
To predict that factories will soon disappear entirely
To prove that robots are too expensive to be useful
To argue that automation policy and choices about sharing gains will determine outcomes
questions.explanation: 末段总结自动化既非纯粹破坏也非轻松进步，结果取决于培训、收益分配和制度适应等选择，故选 D。B、C 与原文不符；A 原文未说工厂会消失。

title: More Than Money: Blockchain's Potential Beyond Cryptocurrency
source: Adapted from financial technology and distributed systems publications
description: 区块链在金融之外的应用潜力
content:
Blockchain first became widely known as the technology behind Bitcoin, and for many people it remains inseparable from the price swings of cryptocurrencies. Yet the underlying idea is more general than any single digital coin. A blockchain is a shared, tamper-resistant record of transactions maintained by a network of computers rather than a central authority. This simple property has attracted interest from industries that need to trust records without relying on a single institution. Banks, retailers, governments, and charities are all experimenting with the technology. This passage looks beyond the speculation to examine where blockchains might genuinely be useful, and what stands in the way.

At its core, a blockchain is a distributed ledger. Instead of one database controlled by one organisation, copies of the record are held by many participants. New entries, often called blocks, are added in a way that all participants can verify. Each block is linked to the previous one using cryptography, so altering an old entry would require changing every later block and persuading the network to accept the change. This makes the record extremely difficult to tamper with. Some blockchains require participants to solve computational puzzles, known as proof of work, while others use different methods to agree on the state of the ledger. The key point is that trust is distributed rather than placed in a single party.

One of the most discussed extensions is the smart contract: a program stored on the blockchain that executes automatically when certain conditions are met. Because the code and its results are visible to all participants, smart contracts can, in principle, reduce the need for intermediaries and lower the cost of enforcement. In insurance, a contract might pay out automatically when a verified weather event occurs. In trade finance, payments could be released as goods move through a supply chain. The appeal is speed and reduced dispute, since the rules are written into the system itself. Critics note, however, that code can contain errors and that rigid automation may be undesirable when circumstances are complex.

Supply chain management is one of the most promising areas. A blockchain can record the journey of a product from its origin to the consumer, creating an audit trail that is hard to falsify. This matters for goods where provenance is important: organic food, fair-trade coffee, diamonds, and pharmaceuticals. A retailer could, in theory, scan an item and show a customer exactly where it came from. During food safety scares, such records could identify the source of contamination far more quickly than paper-based systems. Several large retailers and logistics firms have run trials, although many have found that the hard part is not the technology but persuading every participant to record accurate data in the first place.

In healthcare, blockchains have been proposed as a way to give patients control over their records. A patient could grant permission to a doctor or researcher for a limited time, with each access recorded permanently. This would make it easier to share information between hospitals that use incompatible systems, while preserving a clear audit trail. Some countries have begun to explore national systems based on distributed ledgers. The obstacles are considerable: health records contain sensitive information, and the immutability of a blockchain sits awkwardly with laws that allow patients to have data corrected or erased. Designers are experimenting with storing only references to records rather than the records themselves.

Another application is digital identity. Hundreds of millions of people lack official identification, which prevents them from opening bank accounts, voting, or accessing services. A blockchain-based identity system could give individuals a portable record that they control, independent of any government. Similarly, land registries in many countries are incomplete or corrupt; recording ownership on a tamper-resistant ledger could reduce disputes and make it easier to use property as collateral. Pilot projects have been tried in several developing countries. Yet these schemes raise difficult questions: who verifies that the original entry is true, and how are mistakes corrected if records cannot be changed?

Voting is frequently mentioned as a candidate, but it is also controversial. A blockchain could, in principle, produce a transparent and verifiable count, allowing citizens to check that their vote was recorded. Some cities have experimented with blockchain-based voting in local elections. Most experts, however, remain cautious. Secret ballots are hard to reconcile with a system designed to make transactions visible, and a vote record that can be traced back to an individual undermines privacy. There are also practical concerns about coercing voters and about what happens if a mistake is made. For these reasons, many computer scientists argue that the risks currently outweigh the benefits.

In the energy sector, blockchains are being examined as a tool for managing local electricity markets. Households with solar panels could sell surplus power to neighbours automatically, with a ledger recording each transaction. The technology could also help track renewable energy certificates and carbon credits, making it harder to claim the same credit twice. Some projects have tested peer-to-peer energy trading with encouraging results. Nonetheless, critics point out that a conventional database managed by a regulated utility could often do the same job more efficiently, without the energy cost of maintaining a blockchain.

The technical challenges are substantial. Many blockchains process far fewer transactions per second than established payment networks, and fees can rise sharply when demand is high. Energy consumption is another objection, especially for systems using proof of work, though newer designs consume far less. There is also the problem of interoperability: different blockchains do not easily communicate, and the industry has not settled on common standards. Perhaps most importantly, a blockchain guarantees that recorded data have not been altered, but it cannot guarantee that the data were accurate when entered. As the saying goes, garbage in, garbage out.

The history of the technology illustrates the gap between promise and delivery. At the height of the cryptocurrency boom, companies across many sectors announced blockchain initiatives, and some saw their share prices rise on the announcement alone. Years later, a number of these projects had quietly disappeared, prompting a reassessment. Analysts now distinguish between applications where a shared, tamper-resistant record is genuinely valuable and those where a conventional database would be simpler and cheaper. The more sober view is that blockchain is a useful tool for specific problems, not a universal solution waiting to be applied to everything.

The long-term significance of blockchain is likely to lie in the unglamorous background: verifying records, coordinating between organisations that do not fully trust one another, and reducing the cost of proving that something happened.
