These functions can matter enormously in supply chains, finance, and public administration. Whether the technology fulfils that potential will depend less on price speculation than on careful design, realistic expectations, and rules that protect users. The lesson of the past decade is that the idea is powerful but easily oversold. Used selectively, it may become an important piece of infrastructure; used indiscriminately, it will remain a solution in search of a problem.

questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
options: Blockchain is only useful for cryptocurrencies and has no other value
Blockchain has applications beyond currency but its value is often overstated and depends on suitable use cases
Blockchain technology has completely failed and should be forgotten
Conventional databases can never match any function of a blockchain
questions.explanation: 全文先解释区块链原理，再列举智能合约、供应链、医疗、身份、投票、能源等应用，又用多段指出技术、能耗、数据真实性等局限，末段强调应选择性使用、勿夸大，故主旨为 B。A 与全文众多非货币应用相悖；D 与末段'传统数据库更简单便宜'矛盾。

questions.question: Why is a blockchain difficult to tamper with according to the passage?
options: Because it is stored on a single secure government server
Because each block is linked to the previous one and records are held by many participants
Because all its data are kept secret from users
Because it uses only advanced encryption and no verification
questions.explanation: 第2段说明账本由许多参与者保存副本，每个区块用密码学与前一个相连，篡改旧记录需改动所有后续区块并说服网络，故选 B。A 与'非单一机构控制'相反；C、D 均不符合原文。

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the hardest part of using blockchain in supply chains?
options: Designing a user-friendly scanner
Storing large images on the blockchain
Persuading every participant to record accurate data
Obtaining government approval for each product
questions.explanation: 第4段末尾指出难点不在技术本身，而在于说服每个参与者录入准确数据，故选 C。A、D 文中未提；B 与原文'难点非技术'不符。

questions.question: The word 'immutability' in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: Inability to be changed
High cost of storage
Complete transparency to the public
Freedom from regulation
questions.explanation: 第5段说区块链的 immutability 与允许患者更正或删除数据的法律相冲突，可知该词意为'不可更改性'，故选 A。B、C、D 均与'不可更改'的语义无关。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the author's view of blockchain voting?
options: It is the most promising application and should be adopted widely
It guarantees complete privacy by design
Its transparency conflicts with secrecy of ballots, so caution is warranted
It has already been proven perfectly secure
questions.explanation: 第7段指出多数专家谨慎，因可见的交易记录难以与秘密投票相容、可追溯记录损害隐私，故可推断作者认为透明性与投票保密冲突、应谨慎，选 C。A、D 与'风险大于收益'矛盾；B 与'损害隐私'直接相反。

questions.question: What is the author's main purpose in the last two paragraphs?
options: To encourage speculation in blockchain-related shares
To argue that all databases should be replaced by blockchains
To describe the technical details of proof of work
To urge realistic expectations and selective use rather than indiscriminate adoption
questions.explanation: 倒数第二段区分真正有价值的场景与普通数据库更合适的场景，末段说'有选择地使用'才会成为重要基础设施，故目的在于呼吁现实预期与选择性采用，选 D。A、B 与原文谨慎立场相反；C 只是细节。

title: Learning Anywhere: The Rise of Online Education and MOOCs
source: Adapted from education technology and higher education publications
description: 在线教育与大规模开放在线课程的兴起与争议
content:
For most of history, higher education was bound to a place. Students travelled to a university, sat in lecture halls, and took examinations under supervision. The internet has loosened that link. Today, a learner with a connection can watch lectures from leading professors, complete assignments, and receive certificates without ever setting foot on a campus. Massive open online courses, known as MOOCs, became the most visible symbol of this change when they appeared in the early 2010s. The prospect of cheap, flexible, high-quality education for anyone with a device excited many observers. A decade later, the reality is more nuanced. This passage considers the achievements and the limitations of online learning.

The roots of online education predate the web. Universities had long offered correspondence courses, and in the 1990s many put lecture notes and recordings online. A decisive moment came in 2001, when MIT began publishing the materials of its courses free of charge through its OpenCourseWare project. The development of video platforms and high-speed connections made it possible to reach much larger audiences. In 2012, several American universities launched platforms such as Coursera and edX, offering courses from prestigious institutions to anyone who enrolled. Enrolment numbers were astonishing: a single course could attract hundreds of thousands of learners from around the world.

MOOCs have characteristic features. Courses are typically structured into short video segments interspersed with quizzes and assignments, which are graded automatically. Discussion forums allow participants to ask questions and help one another, creating a sense of community despite the scale. Many courses are free to follow, with optional paid elements such as graded certificates or verified credentials. The best-known platforms host thousands of courses, ranging from computer science and mathematics to philosophy and music. Some are produced by individual universities, others by companies or groups of institutions. The flexibility of studying at one's own pace is particularly attractive to people who work or live far from universities.

The strongest claim made for MOOCs is that they democratise education. A student in a remote town can learn from a professor at a famous university, something impossible a generation ago. For adults who cannot afford to stop working, online study offers a way to gain new skills without giving up income. Courses can be revisited as often as needed, which helps learners who struggle with the pace of a traditional lecture. Some platforms provide subtitles and translations, extending access to non-native speakers and people with hearing difficulties. In fields where knowledge changes quickly, online courses can also be updated faster than printed textbooks.

The most serious criticism concerns completion. Although hundreds of thousands of people may enrol in a popular course, only a small fraction finish it. Early studies suggested completion rates in the single digits, and later research found little improvement. Critics argue that MOOCs are better understood as a form of cheap publishing than as a substitute for a university education. Defenders reply that the metric is misleading: many participants are browsing out of curiosity and may learn a great deal without formally completing the course. They also note that learners who pay for a certificate or have a clear goal are far more likely to finish. The debate reveals how difficult it is to measure learning in an environment where attendance is optional.

Related to completion is the question of interaction. A lecture can be filmed, but the experience of discussing ideas with a teacher and fellow students is harder to reproduce. Online forums can be lively, yet they often lack the structure and continuity of a seminar, and many learners never participate. Some platforms have introduced peer assessment, live sessions, and small study groups to address this gap. Research generally suggests that social presence, the feeling that one is learning alongside others, is an important predictor of success. Courses that build in regular interaction tend to retain more students than those consisting only of videos.

Another obstacle is recognition. Employers and universities have been cautious about accepting MOOC certificates as evidence of learning, partly because the standards of assessment vary and may be weak. Many courses rely on multiple-choice quizzes, which test recall rather than deep understanding. In response, platforms have developed verified certificates involving identity checks and supervised examinations, and some universities now allow MOOC credits to count toward formal degrees. Micro-credentials and online degrees have gained acceptance in certain fields, especially technology. Nevertheless, the prestige of a traditional qualification remains powerful, and a certificate alone rarely transforms a career.

Rather than replacing universities, online tools are increasingly combined with classroom teaching. In a blended or hybrid model, students watch lectures at home and use class time for discussion, problem-solving, and practical work. This approach, sometimes called the flipped classroom, can make better use of contact hours. Some institutions have built entire programmes around a mix of online and residential study. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated this trend, forcing universities to move teaching online almost overnight and prompting a rethinking of what must happen in person. Many students reported that the experience, though imperfect, widened their options.

The digital divide remains a persistent concern. Online learning requires a reliable connection, a suitable device, and a quiet place to study, resources that are not evenly distributed. In poorer countries and rural areas, limited bandwidth can make video-based courses frustrating or impossible. Even within wealthy societies, students from disadvantaged backgrounds may lack the support and study skills that independent learning demands. There is an uncomfortable irony in the claim that education is available to all: those who need it most are often least able to take advantage. Some platforms have responded by offering low-bandwidth versions and mobile-friendly materials.

The rise of online education has also prompted questions about the future of universities. If lectures can be delivered more cheaply online, what justifies the cost of a traditional degree? Some commentators predict that many institutions will struggle, particularly those relying on large undergraduate classes. Others argue that universities offer far more than instruction: they provide community, mentoring, research opportunities, and a credential backed by reputation. The most likely outcome is a period of adaptation, in which universities incorporate online elements while emphasising what cannot be digitised. Competition from technology companies has also pushed institutions to innovate.

Online education has not delivered the total transformation that its early enthusiasts predicted, but it has changed the landscape permanently. It has widened access, created new forms of credential, and forced a re-examination of how teaching is organised. Its weaknesses, including low completion rates and unequal access, are real and not easily solved by technology alone. The most sensible view treats online and classroom learning as complements rather than rivals. Used thoughtfully, they can extend education to people who were previously excluded; used carelessly, they offer the appearance of opportunity without the substance.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: MOOCs have failed completely and should be abandoned
Online learning has expanded access but faces limits, and works best alongside traditional education
Universities will certainly disappear within a decade
Online courses are superior to classroom teaching in every respect
questions.explanation: 全文既讲在线教育扩大 access、形式灵活，又用多段讨论完成率低、互动不足、认证困难、数字鸿沟，末段主张两者互补而非竞争，故主旨为 B。A、C 过于极端且与末段'互补'相悖；D 原文强调局限，未称全面优越。

questions.question: According to the passage, what happened in 2001?
options: Coursera and edX were launched
The COVID-19 pandemic forced universities online
MIT began publishing its course materials free of charge
The first MOOC attracted a million learners
questions.explanation: 第2段明确写道 2001 年 MIT 通过 OpenCourseWare 项目免费公布课程材料，故选 C。A 发生在 2012 年；B 是近年的事；D 原文未提及百万学习者这一具体事件。

questions.question: What does the debate over completion rates reveal?
options: That online courses are always more effective than lectures
That automatic grading has been proved inaccurate
That most learners pay for verified certificates
That it is difficult to measure learning when attendance is optional
questions.explanation: 第5段末指出这场争论揭示在出勤自愿的环境中衡量学习多么困难，故选 D。A 与完成率低的讨论矛盾；B、C 文中无此结论。

questions.question: The word 'democratise' in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: To make something available to all people
To reduce the quality of something
To turn an institution into a business
To restrict access to a privileged group
questions.explanation: 第4段说 MOOCs 最有力的主张是 democratise education，随后举例偏远学生也能向名校教授学习，可知意为'使教育普及、向所有人开放'，故选 A。B、C 与语义无关；D 与原文含义相反。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the flipped classroom?
options: It requires students to attend lectures in person and do homework at school
It uses class time for discussion and practical work after students watch lectures at home
It is a method used only in primary schools
It eliminates the need for any teacher
questions.explanation: 第8段描述混合模式中学生在家看讲座、课堂时间用于讨论与实作，即翻转课堂，故可推断 B 正确。A 把顺序说反；C、D 原文无依据。

questions.question: Which best describes the author's attitude towards online education?
options: Balanced, seeing it as a useful complement with genuine limitations
Completely opposed to any use of technology in education
Certain that it will solve all educational inequality
Convinced that traditional universities have no future
questions.explanation: 末段明确说在线教育未完成彻底变革但永久改变格局，最合理的看法是把线上与课堂视为互补，故作者态度平衡，选 A。C、D 过于绝对；B 与作者承认的诸多效益不符。

title: Educating the Whole Person: The Case for Liberal Arts
source: Adapted from education and humanities publications
description: 通识教育的价值与当代意义
content:
In an age of tight budgets and employment anxiety, universities face pressure to offer qualifications that lead directly to jobs. Subjects seen as practical, such as engineering, computer science, and medicine, attract students and funding, while the liberal arts are often asked to justify their existence. Yet for centuries, a broad education in the arts and sciences was regarded not as a luxury but as the foundation of an educated person. Supporters argue that this tradition is more relevant than ever, because the challenges of the modern world require judgment, communication, and adaptability rather than narrow technical skill. This passage examines the case for educating the whole person.

The liberal arts are not a fixed list of subjects. Historically, they included the trivium of grammar, logic, and rhetoric, and the quadrivium of arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music. Today the term usually refers to a broad curriculum spanning the humanities, social sciences, natural sciences, and the arts, in which students study several disciplines rather than specialising immediately. The underlying idea is that different fields cultivate different ways of thinking, and that an education is incomplete if it develops only one of them. A student might study literature alongside economics, or philosophy alongside biology, learning to move between different kinds of evidence and argument.

The most commonly claimed benefit is the ability to think critically. Studying literature, history, or philosophy requires students to interpret ambiguous texts, weigh competing interpretations, and construct reasoned arguments. Unlike problems with a single correct answer, the questions raised in the humanities often resist final resolution. Students learn to identify assumptions, detect weak reasoning, and distinguish evidence from assertion. These habits are valuable in any field, because the ability to evaluate an unfamiliar claim is more durable than any specific body of knowledge. In a world saturated with information and persuasive messaging, such discernment may be more important than ever.

Closely related is communication. The liberal arts place heavy emphasis on writing and speaking: essays, seminars, presentations, and debate are central to the curriculum. Students learn to organise a complex argument, express it clearly, and respond to criticism. These abilities are consistently ranked among the most sought-after by employers, who often report that graduates possess technical knowledge but struggle to explain it. An engineer who can write a clear report or a scientist who can persuade a non-specialist audience is at a significant advantage. The ability to listen and to make oneself understood underlies leadership and collaboration in nearly every profession.

A third advantage is adaptability. Technical skills can become obsolete within a few years, particularly in fields driven by rapid innovation. A broad education, by contrast, trains people to learn unfamiliar material and to approach problems from multiple angles. Someone who has studied several disciplines is better equipped to change direction, to work in teams with specialists, and to connect ideas that others keep separate. Research on careers suggests that graduates of liberal arts programmes often work in a wide range of occupations, and that their success is not confined to a single path. This flexibility is valuable in labour markets that no one can reliably predict.

The idea has deep roots. The medieval university organised teaching around a common curriculum before students specialised in law, medicine, or theology. In the nineteenth century, reformers such as John Henry Newman defended a broad education on the grounds that it formed character and judgment, not merely skills. In the United States, the liberal arts college became a distinctive institution, and many universities require students to complete a broad distribution of courses before choosing a major. The tradition rests on a vision of education as preparation for a full life, including citizenship and personal fulfilment, rather than preparation for a single job.

In recent decades that vision has come under strain. Tuition fees have risen sharply, and students and families expect a clear return on their investment. Governments increasingly link funding to employment outcomes, and subjects that appear to offer a direct route to a career are favoured. Many liberal arts departments have faced budget cuts or closures. Enrolment patterns have shifted toward fields such as business and computer science. Critics of the traditional curriculum argue that it is too diffuse, that students accumulate credits without depth, and that it fails to provide the practical training that the labour market demands.

The response from supporters is that the economic case is stronger than it appears. Surveys of employers repeatedly place communication, critical thinking, and problem-solving at the top of the list of desired skills. Studies comparing the earnings of graduates suggest that the gap between liberal arts and vocational subjects is smaller than commonly assumed, and that it narrows over a career. Liberal arts graduates are well represented in management, law, education, publishing, and public service. The more immediate difficulty is that these outcomes are hard to demonstrate at the point of entry, when a student must decide what to study. A degree in a vocational field promises a clear first job; a broad education promises a capacity to keep growing.

The strongest versions of the liberal arts tradition do not deny the value of specialisation. Most programmes allow students to pursue a major in depth while also completing a broad set of requirements. The aim is to produce a mind that is both focused and wide-ranging, able to see the details of a subject and its relation to larger questions. Interdisciplinary courses, which combine methods from several fields, have become especially popular. Scholars argue that the most important advances often occur at the boundaries between disciplines, where someone trained in one field asks a question that specialists in another have overlooked.

Beyond employment, there is a civic and ethical dimension. A broad education introduces students to unfamiliar cultures, historical experiences, and ways of life, which can foster empathy and make aggressive simplification harder. The study of ethics, politics, and history provides a vocabulary for discussing public questions. Defenders see this as essential to a functioning democracy, which depends on citizens who can evaluate arguments and resist demagoguery. Critics may regard such claims as vague, but the concern is a serious one: a society of narrowly trained specialists may possess great technical capacity while lacking the wisdom to direct it.

The case for the liberal arts is not that every student should study them to the exclusion of everything else, but that a university education should leave room for breadth. The habits cultivated by studying across disciplines, careful reading, clear expression, and openness to unfamiliar ideas, remain valuable long after particular facts have faded. In a world of rapid change and uncertain employment, the capacity to think and to communicate may be the most practical asset of all. The challenge for universities is to preserve these benefits while making their value visible to students who are understandably anxious about the future.

questions.question: What is the central argument of this passage?
options: A broad liberal education cultivates durable skills and should remain part of university study despite modern pressures
Specialised technical training is always superior to a broad education
The liberal arts should replace all professional degree programmes
Universities should admit only students who already know their future career
questions.explanation: 全文论证通识教育培养批判思维、沟通与适应能力，回应就业与经费压力，末段主张大学应留出广度空间，故主旨为 A。B 与全文立场相反；C 过于极端，原文并不否认专业化；D 原文无此主张。

questions.question: According to the passage, what did the historical trivium include?
options: Arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music
Grammar, logic and rhetoric
Engineering, medicine and law
Literature, economics and biology
questions.explanation: 第2段明确指出 trivium 包括语法、逻辑与修辞，而四艺才包含算术、几何、天文与音乐，故选 B。A 是 quadrivium 的内容；C、D 是后文举例的现代学科，均非 trivium。

questions.question: Which skills do employers repeatedly rank highly according to the passage?
options: Memorisation of facts and rapid calculation
Manual dexterity and physical strength
Communication, critical thinking and problem-solving
Knowledge of a single specialised software package
questions.explanation: 第8段指出雇主调查反复把沟通、批判性思维与解决问题能力列在最受追捧技能之首，故选 C。A、B、D 均与原文列举的技能不符。

questions.question: The word 'obsolete' in the passage is closest in meaning to which of the following?
options: Highly respected
Out of date and no longer useful
Difficult to learn
Universally available
questions.explanation: 第5段说技术技能在快速创新领域几年内就可能 obsolete，结合'通识教育培养学习能力'的对比可知意为'过时、不再有用'，故选 B。A、C 与本段语义无关；D 与'过时'相反。

questions.question: What can be inferred about interdisciplinary courses from the passage?
options: They prevent students from specialising in any field
They are less popular than single-subject courses
They are designed only for students who fail other courses
They are valued because important advances often happen at boundaries between disciplines
questions.explanation: 第9段说跨学科课程很受欢迎，学者认为最重要的进展常发生在学科边界，故可推断 D 正确。B 与原文'尤其受欢迎'相反；A 原文说学生仍可深入主修。

questions.question: Which best describes the author's attitude towards the liberal arts?
options: Defensive but admitting they have no practical value
Supportive, while recognising the pressures universities face
Dismissive of traditional curricula
Neutral, with no clear position
questions.explanation: 作者既回应就业与经费压力，又强调通识教育的持久价值，末段呼吁在承认学生焦虑的同时保留广度，故为支持但正视现实，选 B。A 与作者强调实用性矛盾；D 与全文鲜明立场不符。

title: The First Years: Why Early Childhood Education Matters
source: Adapted from education research and child development publications
description: 幼儿教育对儿童发展的重要性
content:
The first years of a child's life were once regarded as a private matter, the exclusive concern of families and the newborn's immediate circle. Today, economists, neuroscientists and policymakers increasingly view them as the most consequential period in human development. The reason is a growing body of research showing that the brain develops more rapidly in the first five years than at any other time, and that the experiences a child encounters in this window shape cognitive ability, emotional regulation and even physical health for decades afterwards. Early childhood education has consequently moved from the margins of social policy to its centre. This passage examines the evidence for its importance, the forms it takes, and the debates about how societies should provide it.

The scientific case rests above all on the phenomenon of neural plasticity. At birth, a human brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons, but the connections between them are relatively sparse. During the first years, these neurons form synapses at an extraordinary rate, peaking at around two years of age, when a child may have more than twice as many synaptic connections as an adult. The brain then prunes the pathways that are rarely used and strengthens those that are repeatedly activated. This process is experience-dependent: a child who is spoken to, read to and stimulated builds a richer network than one who is neglected. Neuroscientists therefore speak of sensitive periods, windows in which particular capacities are especially easy to acquire. Language and emotional attachment are thought to have such windows, and missing them does not make learning impossible, but it makes it considerably harder.

The flip side of plasticity is vulnerability. Toxic stress, the prolonged activation of the body's stress-response systems in the absence of a supportive adult, can disrupt developing brain circuitry. Studies have linked chronic exposure to poverty, violence or neglect to elevated levels of cortisol, which in turn is associated with smaller volume in the hippocampus, a region vital for memory, and with difficulties in impulse control. Children growing up in such conditions often enter school already behind their more advantaged peers, not because they lack ability but because their early environment has shaped the tools they bring to learning. This finding is central to the argument for early intervention: it suggests that many later educational inequalities have their roots in experiences that precede formal schooling.

High-quality early childhood education is designed to counteract precisely these disadvantages. Programmes for children aged three to five typically combine structured language activities, numeracy games, music, art and guided play with careful attention to social interaction. Crucially, they also offer a stable, nurturing relationship with trained caregivers, which helps children develop what psychologists call secure attachment. A securely attached child is more willing to explore, more able to manage frustration, and better equipped to form relationships with teachers and peers. In this sense, early education is not simply about teaching letters and numbers; it is about building the emotional foundations on which all later learning depends.

The strongest evidence for lasting effects comes from longitudinal studies that have followed children into adulthood. The Perry Preschool Project, launched in the 1960s in Michigan, provided high-quality pre-schooling and home visits to a small group of disadvantaged children. Decades later, researchers found that participants were more likely to graduate from high school, less likely to be arrested, and earned more than a control group. The Abecedarian Project in North Carolina, which began intervention even earlier and continued longer, reported similar gains in educational attainment and employment. Such studies are not without limitations: their samples were small, and it is difficult to separate the effect of the programme from that of the wider support the families received. Nevertheless, their consistency has been influential.

Economists have translated these findings into arguments about public spending. The Nobel laureate James Heckman has argued that investment in early childhood yields one of the highest economic returns of any social policy, because it is far cheaper to build skills in a three-year-old than to remediate their absence in a thirty-year-old. His analyses suggest that every dollar spent on high-quality early education can save several dollars in later costs, including welfare payments, remedial education and incarceration. A World Bank study of a pre-school programme in Chile reached a comparable conclusion, finding benefits that outweighed costs many times over. These calculations have persuaded governments across the world to expand pre-school provision, although the quality of that provision varies enormously.

Beyond cognitive and economic outcomes, early childhood education plays a vital role in social and emotional learning. In a well-run classroom, children learn to take turns, to articulate their feelings, to resolve disputes without violence and to persist at a task that is difficult. These capacities, often grouped under the term executive function, include working memory, inhibitory control and flexible thinking. Research has shown that executive function in childhood predicts academic achievement and even adult health and wealth more reliably than IQ alone. The reason may be that academic success depends as much on the ability to concentrate and to delay gratification as on raw intelligence. A curriculum that neglects these skills in favour of rote instruction may therefore be counterproductive.

This is why many educators defend the place of play in early education. To an adult, a child absorbed in building a tower or inventing an imaginary world may appear to be wasting time. In fact, such activities are the means through which young children test hypotheses, practise language and learn to cooperate. When a group of children negotiates the rules of a game, they are engaging in sophisticated social reasoning. When they stack blocks and watch them fall, they are exploring cause and effect. Play-based programmes, common in Scandinavia and increasingly influential elsewhere, seek to harness this natural learning process, providing rich environments and skilled adults who extend children's thinking without taking control of it.

Not all early childhood provision, however, delivers these benefits. Researchers emphasise that quality is decisive. A pre-school with well-trained, well-paid teachers, small group sizes, a stimulating curriculum and strong links to parents produces lasting gains; a merely custodial setting, in which children are kept safe but little else, may produce none. The difference often comes down to the quality of the interactions between adults and children. Studies using the Classroom Assessment Scoring System have found that emotional support, classroom organisation and instructional support predict children's development more strongly than do physical facilities or formal qualifications alone. This has led to calls for better training and lower staff turnover, since children form attachments to particular caregivers and suffer when those caregivers repeatedly leave.

The family remains the child's first and most influential educator, and no programme can substitute entirely for a supportive home. Reading aloud to a child, conversing at meals and responding warmly to distress all build the same neural circuits that pre-schooling aims to strengthen. Some of the most effective interventions therefore work with parents rather than replacing them, offering home visits, parenting classes and advice on nutrition and stimulation. The most successful combine centre-based education with support for the family, recognising that a child's development is shaped by several environments at once. This also explains why programmes that reach only the most disadvantaged children can struggle: they may fail to change the wider circumstances to which those children return each afternoon.

These considerations feed into a long-running policy debate about whether early education should be universal or targeted. Advocates of universal provision argue that it reduces stigma, builds social mixing and attracts greater political support, since middle-class families also use the system and therefore defend its funding. Advocates of targeting counter that resources are limited and should be concentrated where the need and the potential return are greatest. In practice, many countries adopt a hybrid model, offering a universal foundation while providing additional support for disadvantaged areas. Countries such as Finland and New Zealand have made substantial public investment in early years, while others, including parts of the United States, rely on a patchwork of private and publicly funded provision that leaves many families without affordable options.

In conclusion, the case for early childhood education rests on a convergence of evidence from neuroscience, psychology and economics. The first years lay down the architecture of the brain, establish patterns of emotional response and set the trajectory of later learning. High-quality programmes can improve outcomes for individuals and yield substantial returns for society, but only when they are genuinely high in quality and sensitive to the child's family context. The challenge for policymakers is therefore not simply to provide more pre-schools, but to ensure that every child, regardless of circumstance, has access to the kind of early experience in which a young mind can flourish.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Early childhood education shapes brain, emotional and social development and deserves serious public investment
Most children are born with identical abilities and only schooling creates differences
Formal academic instruction should begin as early as possible in every country
Parents have little influence compared with professional educators
questions.explanation: 全文从神经可塑性、情感依恋、长期追踪研究、经济效益、游戏与质量等角度论证幼儿教育对儿童发展的深远意义，并在结尾呼吁公共投入与质量保障，故主旨为 A。B 与原文所述早期环境差异相悖；C 曲解原文，作者强调游戏与社会情感而非尽早灌输学术知识；D 与第9段'家庭是第一位且最有影响力的教育者'矛盾。

questions.question: According to the passage, what happens in the brain during the first years of life?
options: The number of neurons steadily declines until adulthood
Synapses form rapidly and are then pruned according to experience
The hippocampus stops growing after the age of two
Cortisol production becomes permanently switched off
questions.explanation: 第2段指出神经元在生命最初几年以惊人速度形成突触，约两岁时达到峰值，随后大脑会修剪少用的通路、强化常用的通路，且这一过程受经验影响，故选 B。A 错，原文说神经元数量约 860 亿但初期突触稀疏，并非神经元减少；C 原文只说压力会影响海马体体积，未称其停止生长；D 与原文慢性压力下皮质醇升高相反。

questions.question: The word 'custodial' in paragraph 9 is closest in meaning to
options: Highly stimulating and intellectually rich
Run by trained teachers with low staff turnover
Designed specifically for disadvantaged families
Concerned only with keeping children safe
questions.explanation: 第9段将高质量幼儿园与 'merely custodial setting' 对比，后者 'in which children are kept safe but little else'，即只负责看护安全、缺乏教育刺激，故 custodial 意为'仅看护的'，选 D。A 与原文'little else'相反；B 描述的是高质量机构特征；C 文中未把看护型机构限定于弱势家庭。

questions.question: What can be inferred about executive function from the passage?
options: It is fixed at birth and cannot be improved by education
It matters less than IQ for predicting later success
It can be developed through social interaction and predicts later achievement
It is only relevant to children from disadvantaged backgrounds
questions.explanation: 第7段说明执行功能包括工作记忆、抑制控制和灵活思维，可在课堂互动中习得，且比智商更能预测学业与成年健康财富，故可推断 C 正确。A 与'可学习'矛盾；B 与'比 IQ 更可靠预测'相反；D 原文称其对所有儿童都重要，并非仅限弱势儿童。

questions.question: What is the author's attitude towards play-based early education?
options: Sceptical, because play wastes valuable learning time
Indifferent, treating it as an unproven fashion
Critical, because it lacks any structured curriculum
Favourable, seeing it as a natural way children learn
questions.explanation: 第8段作者明确为游戏辩护，称搭建积木、协商规则是在检验假设、练习语言和社会推理，并说斯堪的纳维亚的游戏本位课程颇具影响力，故态度是支持的，选 D。A、C 与作者论述相反；B 与作者积极引述研究和实例不符。

questions.question: What is the purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To argue that pre-school should be made compulsory by law
To summarise the evidence and call for high-quality, accessible provision
To criticise economists for studying early education
To describe the history of pre-school in Scandinavia
questions.explanation: 末段总结神经科学、心理学与经济学的证据汇聚，指出高质量项目有益，并呼吁让每个孩子都能获得优质早期经验，即总结证据并呼吁优质、普及的供给，故选 B。A 未提强制入学；C 错，作者引用经济学家是为支持论点而非批评；D 未在末段叙述北欧历史。

title: Testing Times: The Debate Over Standardized Exams
source: Adapted from education policy and assessment publications
description: 标准化考试的优劣之争
content:
Few educational tools are as familiar, or as controversial, as the standardized exam. At some point in almost every schooling system, students sit down with a pencil or a keyboard and answer the same questions under the same conditions as thousands of their peers. Supporters regard these tests as the fairest way to measure learning and to hold schools accountable. Critics see them as a crude instrument that narrows the curriculum, rewards rote memorisation and inflicts needless anxiety. The debate is not merely technical: it reflects competing visions of what education is for. This passage examines the uses of standardized testing, the case made against it, and the alternatives that have been proposed.

Standardized tests are assessments administered and scored in a consistent, predetermined way. Every candidate faces the same questions, the same time limits and the same marking criteria, so that results can be compared across schools, districts and years. Their modern form emerged in the early twentieth century, when psychologists such as Alfred Binet developed intelligence scales and educators began to apply statistical methods to measurement. During the Second World War, the United States Army used group tests to sort recruits, and after the war the practice spread rapidly into schools and universities. Today, examinations such as the SAT, the GCSE and countless national tests shape the progress of millions of students and the funding of thousands of schools.

The case for standardization begins with comparability. When every student answers the same questions, a grade in one school means roughly the same as a grade in another, allowing universities and employers to make decisions with some confidence. Subjective assessment, by contrast, can vary markedly between markers; an essay praised by one teacher might be marked down by another. Standardized tests, particularly those composed of multiple-choice items, can be scored with near-perfect reliability and at low cost. They also provide governments with data: aggregated results reveal which schools are improving, which are failing and where additional resources are needed. In this view, testing is an essential instrument of accountability and of equity, because it makes hidden differences visible.

For advocates, standardized exams also promote fairness. Because the questions and conditions are identical, the influence of a teacher's personal bias or a school's reputation is reduced. Some supporters point out that tests can expose the underperformance of schools serving disadvantaged communities, which might otherwise be overlooked. The physicist Richard Feynman, writing about California's textbook controversies, argued that standardized testing could help identify whether pupils were actually learning to read, rather than simply being passed from grade to grade. The underlying principle is that measurement, however imperfect, is preferable to no measurement at all: without it, the educational system cannot judge its own effectiveness.

Yet the criticisms are substantial and have grown louder. The first is that high-stakes testing narrows the curriculum. When a school's funding, a teacher's bonus or a student's promotion depends on results in mathematics and literacy, there is a powerful incentive to devote classroom time to those subjects at the expense of history, art, music and science. This phenomenon, often described as 'teaching to the test', encourages drilling in the precise formats the exam uses. Teachers report that the pressure to cover the syllabus leaves little room for discussion, creativity or the exploration of unexpected questions. In extreme cases, schools have been found to exclude low-performing students from testing altogether in order to raise their average scores.

A second objection concerns the effect on students' mental health. The anticipation of a single examination that will determine university admission or graduation can produce severe anxiety, particularly among young people who have learned to define their worth by grades. Researchers have documented elevated levels of stress hormones during examination periods and have linked high-stakes testing to sleep disturbance and school avoidance. Critics argue that a system which repeatedly tells adolescents that their future depends on a few hours of performance teaches them that learning is a competition rather than a process of discovery. They also note that the pressure falls unevenly, since affluent families can afford private tutoring while poorer students often cannot.

A third line of attack focuses on bias and cultural fairness. A test item may appear neutral while in fact assuming familiarity with a particular culture's vocabulary, experiences or ways of reasoning. A question about, say, a regatta or a ski resort may advantage students from families that have encountered such things. Psychologists use the term 'cultural loading' for this problem, and despite decades of effort to write items free of it, complete neutrality may be impossible. There is also evidence of stereotype threat: when students are reminded of a negative stereotype about their social group before a test, their performance can decline. Standardization, critics conclude, may standardise disadvantage as much as opportunity.

Validity is a further technical concern. A test is valid if it measures what it claims to measure, and reliable if it produces consistent results. A multiple-choice examination can be highly reliable yet fail to assess deeper understanding, original thought or the ability to construct an argument. Because such higher-order skills are difficult and expensive to mark, they are often squeezed out of standardized formats. This creates a mismatch between what schools say they value and what they actually test. As the educational philosopher Sir Ken Robinson argued, systems tend to measure the easiest things rather than the most important ones, and then congratulate themselves on the results.

In response, many countries have experimented with alternative forms of assessment. Continuous assessment, in which coursework and classroom performance accumulate over a term, reduces the.weight of any single sitting and gives teachers more freedom to design rich tasks. Portfolio assessment asks students to collect examples of their work over time, demonstrating growth as well as attainment. Oral examinations and practical projects can test skills that written papers miss. Some systems combine several methods, using standardized tests as one component among many. Finland, frequently cited in this context, relies relatively little on standardized testing, yet consistently performs well in international comparisons, a fact that critics of high-stakes testing regard as powerful evidence.

Advocates of reform, however, face their own difficulties. Alternatives are usually more expensive to administer and harder to standardise, raising the old problem of fairness between markers. Coursework can be written by parents or purchased from essay mills, and a student's performance may depend heavily on the quality of their teacher. When schools have a financial interest in high grades, coursework may be graded more generously, a phenomenon known as grade inflation. For these reasons, some countries that abandoned external examinations have later reintroduced them. The challenge is to design a system that captures the richness of a student's ability without sacrificing comparability or inviting manipulation.

The role of examinations in university admissions illustrates the tension particularly clearly. Standardized scores offer admissions tutors a common yardstick for applicants from thousands of different schools, and in countries with large applicant pools this is administratively attractive. Yet universities have repeatedly found that scores alone are weak predictors of degree performance, especially when compared with prior grades in relevant subjects. Some institutions have therefore made testing optional or removed it altogether, arguing that it adds little beyond the school transcript. Others worry that dropping tests makes admissions more dependent on factors such as family background and the reputation of a student's school, reducing rather than increasing fairness.

The debate over standardized exams is unlikely to be settled by a single decisive study, because both sides are defending genuine values. Fairness, accountability and comparability are real goods; so are creativity, depth of understanding and the psychological welfare of students. The most promising path is probably not to abolish testing but to improve it: to use a balanced range of methods, to write items that are demonstrably free of bias, to report results in ways that encourage improvement rather than punishment, and to ensure that no single examination carries the weight of a whole future. Education, after all, is too important to be reduced to a number, but it is also too important to be left entirely unmeasured.

questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the author's overall position?
options: Standardized exams should be abolished immediately in every country
Testing measures only rote learning and has no legitimate purpose
Exams have real benefits but should be improved and balanced with other methods
Universities rely on exam scores because they are the best predictor of success
questions.explanation: 全文先陈述标准化考试的公平性、可比性与问责价值，再列举课程窄化、焦虑、文化偏差与效度问题，末段主张'不废除而是改良'、采用多元评价，故主旨为 C（考试有真实益处但应改良并与其他方法平衡）。A 过于极端，作者明确反对立刻废除；B 与末段改良主张相悖；D 与第10段'分数单独预测力弱'相反。

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the main argument in favour of standardized testing?
options: It allows results to be compared fairly across different schools
It is the cheapest way to assess creative thinking
It completely eliminates the influence of family background
It reduces the amount of time teachers spend in classrooms
questions.explanation: 第3段指出标准化测试的核心优势是可比性：同一套题目让不同学校、地区、年份的成绩具有可比性，且评分可靠、成本低，故选 A。B 错，原文说深层与创造性思维难以用标准化形式测量；C 错，作者承认偏差仍存在，不能消除家庭背景影响；D 原文未提及。

questions.question: What does 'teaching to the test' most probably mean in paragraph 5?
options: Designing examinations that test higher-order thinking
Focusing classroom time on the exact formats the exam will use
Allowing students to sit the exam more than once
Training teachers to mark papers consistently
questions.explanation: 第5段称高利害考试促使教师把课堂时间集中于考试题型、反复操练（drilling in the precise formats the exam uses），故 'teaching to the test' 指围绕考试题型安排教学，选 B。A 恰与原文相反，原文说深层思维被挤占；C 未提及；D 是评分一致性，并非该短语含义。

questions.question: Which point is used by the author to illustrate the problem of cultural bias in tests?
options: The use of multiple-choice items makes marking highly reliable
Finland performs well despite limited standardized testing
Coursework can be written by parents or purchased online
A question about a regatta may favour students familiar with it
questions.explanation: 第7段举例说 'a question about, say, a regatta or a ski resort may advantage students from families that have encountered such things'，用以说明文化负载问题，故选 D。A 属于支持考试可靠性的论点；B 是替代评价的证据；C 是课程作业的弊端，均与文化偏差无关。

questions.question: What can be inferred about universities' use of admissions tests?
options: They consider test scores the single best predictor of degree performance
They have all stopped using any form of standardized assessment
They use scores mainly to identify students from wealthy families
They value a common yardstick but increasingly doubt the tests' added value
questions.explanation: 第10段说明标准化分数为来自不同学校的申请者提供共同尺度、行政上便利，但大学又发现分数单独预测学位表现的能力弱，有些学校因此改为可选或取消，故可推断大学既看重统一标准又日益怀疑其附加价值，选 D。A 与原文'弱预测力'相反；B 过于绝对，原文只说有些大学；C 曲解原意。

questions.question: What is the purpose of mentioning Sir Ken Robinson in the passage?
options: To show that examinations are popular with students
To support the idea that systems measure easy things rather than important ones
To argue that science subjects should be tested more often
To criticise the use of statistical methods in education
questions.explanation: 第8段引用 Sir Ken Robinson 的话 'systems tend to measure the easiest things rather than the most important ones'，用以支持标准化考试可能测不到深层能力的论点，故选 B。A 与引用语境相反；C 未提及；D 与原文无关，作者并未批评统计方法。

title: Never Too Late: The Importance of Lifelong Learning
source: Adapted from adult education and workforce development publications
description: 终身学习在知识经济时代的必要性
content:
Not long ago, education was imagined as a bounded phase of life. A person went to school, perhaps to university, and then entered a working world in which the knowledge acquired in youth could be expected to last for decades. That assumption has collapsed. In the knowledge economy of the twenty-first century, the half-life of a professional skill — the time it takes for half of what one knows to become obsolete — has shrunk dramatically. Estimates suggest that the skills required for many occupations now change by more than a third within a decade. The consequence is straightforward but profound: learning can no longer be confined to the first years of life. It has become a continuous necessity, and the phrase 'lifelong learning' has moved from educational jargon to economic common sense.

The forces driving this change are well documented. Technological innovation is the most visible. Automation has long replaced routine manual labour, and advances in artificial intelligence now encroach on tasks once thought to require judgement and expertise. A software developer who trained a decade ago may find that the languages, frameworks and tools of youth have been superseded. A accountant must keep pace with changing tax law and new accounting standards. A nurse must master new treatments and new technologies at the bedside. In each case, the credential that once certified competence is no longer sufficient on its own; what matters is the capacity to update it repeatedly.

Demography reinforces the trend. People are living longer and, in many countries, retiring later. A sixty-five-year-old in good health may spend another twenty years in the workforce, a period longer than the entire school-to-university journey of a younger colleague. At the same time, birth rates in many wealthy nations are falling, so the pool of young workers available to replace older ones is shrinking. Economists argue that extending working lives is essential to sustain pension systems and public finances. But longer careers are only viable if older workers can adapt their skills. Lifelong learning is therefore not merely a matter of personal fulfilment; it is a structural requirement of ageing societies.

Lifelong learning takes many forms, and it is important not to equate it with formal study. The OECD distinguishes three categories. Formal learning occurs in structured settings such as schools, colleges and universities and leads to recognised qualifications. Non-formal learning is organised but less institutionally embedded: a workplace training course, a professional workshop, a community class. Informal learning is the unplanned accumulation of knowledge through daily experience, conversation, reading and experimentation. Much of what people actually learn at work is informal, picked up from colleagues and from solving problems. A useful attitude to lifelong learning recognises the value of all three rather than privileging qualifications alone.

For the individual, the benefits are considerable. The most obvious is employability. Workers who continually update their skills are more likely to find work, to command higher wages and to recover quickly from unemployment. Research from the European Union has found that adults who participate in training earn a significant premium over those who do not, and that the premium grows with the intensity of the training. Equally important is resilience: a versatile worker can move between roles and industries as demand shifts. In an economy characterised by disruption, the ability to learn may be a more durable asset than any specific technical skill. As one career adviser put it, the safest specialisation is learning itself.

The advantages are not purely economic. Engaging in new learning keeps the mind active, and a growing body of research links continued intellectual stimulation to better cognitive outcomes in later life. Adults who study a language, learn an instrument or take up a new subject report greater confidence and a stronger sense of purpose. Learning also introduces people to new ideas and new communities, countering the narrowing of horizons that can accompany years in a single profession. For retired people in particular, a course or a study group can provide structure, companionship and a reason to engage with the world. The motivational roots of adult learning, as the psychologist Malcolm Knowles argued, differ from those of children: adults learn best when the material is relevant to their own goals and when they are treated as autonomous partners in the process.

Society as a whole gains too. Well-educated adults are more likely to vote, to volunteer, to trust their neighbours and to make informed health choices. These forms of social capital underpin the functioning of democracies and communities. Lifelong learning can also ease the friction of social change: when immigrants take language classes, when displaced workers retrain, when citizens learn to evaluate information critically, the result is a more adaptable and cohesive society. For this reason, several governments have framed adult education not as a private luxury but as a public investment with wide spillover benefits.

Despite the consensus about its importance, participation is uneven, and the barriers are stubborn. Time is the most frequently cited obstacle: adults juggling work, childcare and household responsibilities struggle to find hours for study. Cost is another, particularly for those who must pay fees themselves. Yet psychological barriers may be more limiting than practical ones. Many adults carry memories of school failure and believe, wrongly, that their capacity to learn has declined with age. Others simply do not know what opportunities exist or how to access them. Unsurprisingly, participation is highest among the already well educated and the well paid — precisely the groups that need it least — a pattern that sociologists describe as the Matthew effect, in which the advantaged accumulate further advantage.

Employers have a crucial role to play. Many companies now invest heavily in internal training, recognising that a skilled workforce is a competitive asset. SAP, for example, has built extensive online learning platforms for its employees, while other firms offer tuition reimbursement for external study. The most forward-looking organisations treat learning as part of the working day rather than an optional extra, since evidence suggests that short, frequent bursts of training are more effective than occasional intensive courses. However, there is a tension here: firms that invest in general skills may find that trained employees leave for competitors. This can discourage investment, especially in sectors with high turnover, and strengthens the case for a wider public system that does not depend on any single employer.

Governments have responded in various ways. Some subsidise adult education directly; others create frameworks for recognising prior learning, so that skills acquired informally can be formally credited. Micro-credentials — short, focused certifications in a particular competency — have proliferated, offering a more flexible alternative to a full degree. Online learning has dramatically widened access: a farmer in a remote region can now study agricultural science through a university course delivered by video, and a parent can complete a qualification in the evening. Yet the digital divide remains real. Effective lifelong learning policy must therefore combine online provision with local, face-to-face support, and must ensure that guidance is available to those who need it most.

Looking to the future, the demand for continual learning is likely to intensify rather than diminish. As automation handles more routine work, the distinctly human capacities — creativity, empathy, complex communication — will become more valuable, and these too must be cultivated and refreshed. The old model of education as a preparation for life has been replaced by a different idea: education as a dimension of life itself. This shift asks something of institutions, which must become more flexible and welcoming to learners of all ages. But it also asks something of individuals, who must be willing to remain learners even when it is inconvenient. The reward is a working life that is not merely endured but continually remade.

In conclusion, lifelong learning is no longer an optional ornament to a career but a central requirement of the modern economy and of a society facing demographic change. It brings economic rewards, protects cognitive health and strengthens the fabric of community life. The obstacles — time, cost, low confidence and unequal access — are real but not insurmountable. The task is to build systems that make learning accessible at every stage of life, and to cultivate in people the belief that it is never, in fact, too late to begin.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: Universities should lower their entry standards for older students
Lifelong learning is mainly a way to fill the hours after retirement
Continuous learning has become an economic and social necessity, though access remains unequal
Technological change has made all traditional qualifications completely worthless
questions.explanation: 全文围绕知识经济中技能折旧、人口老龄化、个人与社会收益、参与障碍与政策应对展开，末段总结终身学习是经济社会必需但获取仍不平等，故选 C。A 原文未提降低大学门槛；B 把终身学习窄化为退休消遣，与原文强调就业能力相悖；D 过于绝对，原文说资格证书'alone'不足，而非完全无用。

questions.question: What does the passage say about the 'half-life' of a professional skill?
options: It has remained constant for several decades
It has become much shorter as knowledge changes rapidly
It refers to the length of a professional training course
It is longest in occupations involving new technology
questions.explanation: 第1段指出 'the half-life of a professional skill — the time it takes for half of what one knows to become obsolete — has shrunk dramatically'，即技能折旧期大幅缩短，故选 B。A 与'shrunk'相反；C 曲解定义；D 原文未比较行业长短，且技术行业变化更快，折旧期应更短。

questions.question: The word 'obsolete' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: Out of date and no longer useful
Highly prized by employers
Difficult to learn in adulthood
Formally recognised by a university
questions.explanation: 第1段把 half-life 定义为'一个人所知的一半变得 obsolete 所需的时间'，结合上下文技能快速过时，obsolete 意为'过时的、不再有用的'，故选 A。B 与语境相反；C、D 均不符合该词在此处的含义。

questions.question: What can be inferred about employers' attitudes towards training?
options: They generally refuse to invest in any form of staff development
They prefer a single intensive course to short, frequent training
They regard training purely as a legal obligation
They may underinvest in general skills because trained staff can leave
questions.explanation: 第9段指出企业虽重视培训，但投资通用技能后员工可能跳槽到竞争对手处，这种顾虑会抑制投资，故可推断 D 正确。A 与原文列举的 SAP 等公司大量投资相悖；B 与原文'短时高频培训更有效'相反；C 原文未提及法律义务。

questions.question: What is the author's attitude towards online learning?
options: Enthusiastic, believing it solves every access problem
Cautiously positive, recognising wider access but also the digital divide
Hostile, because it cannot replace face-to-face teaching
Indifferent, treating it as a passing trend
questions.explanation: 第10段肯定在线学习'widened access'，同时指出'digital divide remains real'、需配合线下支持，故态度是谨慎乐观，选 B。A 忽略作者指出的数字鸿沟；C 与作者肯定态度不符；D 与作者详细讨论相悖。

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To summarise the case for lifelong learning and identify remaining challenges
To announce a new government policy on adult education
To argue that retirement should be abolished
To compare education systems in different countries
questions.explanation: 末段总结终身学习的经济、认知与社会价值，并指出时间、成本、信心与机会不均等障碍仍需应对，即总结论点并点明剩余挑战，故选 A。B 未宣布具体政策；C 曲解原文（原文说退休年龄延后）；D 未在末段做跨国比较。

title: Two Tongues, One Mind: The Benefits of Bilingual Education
source: Adapted from linguistics and education research publications
description: 双语教育的认知与社会益处
content:
In many parts of the world, speaking two languages is an ordinary fact of daily life. Estimates suggest that more than half of the world's population uses two or more languages in everyday communication. Yet in education, bilingualism has often been treated as a problem to be managed rather than an asset to be cultivated. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, many schools punished children for speaking their home language, on the assumption that it interfered with the acquisition of the dominant tongue. Recent research has overturned this view. A growing body of evidence suggests that bilingual education can enhance cognitive flexibility, improve academic outcomes and strengthen social understanding. This passage explores the forms bilingual education takes and the benefits and challenges associated with it.

Bilingual programmes vary widely in their design. In submersion programmes, students are placed in mainstream classes taught entirely in the majority language, with little or no support for their first language. Transitional programmes use the home language temporarily as a bridge, gradually replacing it with the majority language. Immersion programmes, by contrast, teach minority-language speakers largely in the majority language from the outset, while dual-language or two-way immersion programmes educate speakers of both languages together, with instruction delivered in each. Maintenance programmes aim to develop full proficiency in the home language alongside the second. The effectiveness of a programme depends heavily on which of these models is adopted and on how well it is implemented.

The strongest claims for bilingual education concern cognition. Because a bilingual person must manage two competing language systems, the brain develops mechanisms for selecting the appropriate one and suppressing the other. Psychologists describe this as executive control, a set of processes that includes inhibiting irrelevant information, switching between tasks and holding information in working memory. Numerous studies have found that bilingual children outperform monolingual peers on tasks requiring such control. In a classic experiment, children were asked to name the ink colour of words that spelled out a different colour — the Stroop task. Bilinguals were better at resisting the automatic tendency to read the word, suggesting more efficient attentional control.

Neuroimaging research lends support to these behavioural findings. Brain scans have shown that bilingual individuals may have denser grey matter in regions involved in language control and executive function, such as the anterior cingulate cortex and the basal ganglia. Some studies also suggest that bilingualism can delay the onset of dementia symptoms by several years, apparently because the constant management of two languages builds cognitive reserve — a cushion of neural efficiency that compensates for age-related damage. These findings are not universally replicated, and researchers caution that results depend on factors such as age of acquisition and proficiency. Nevertheless, the overall pattern has been influential in reframing bilingualism as a source of mental flexibility rather than confusion.

Bilingualism also appears to foster metalinguistic awareness: an understanding of language as a system that can be analysed and manipulated. A child who knows that the same object can be called by two different names is more likely to grasp that words are arbitrary symbols, a insight that supports literacy. Studies have found that bilingual children often outperform monolinguals on tasks involving phonological awareness — the ability to identify and manipulate the sounds of speech — which is a strong predictor of reading success. This helps explain why well-designed bilingual programmes do not, as critics once claimed, retard literacy in the majority language. On the contrary, strong skills in the first language frequently transfer to the second.

The academic evidence is reassuring on this point. Early studies sometimes reported lower test scores for bilingual pupils, but many of these failed to control for socioeconomic status and used tests administered only in the majority language. When researchers compare like with like, the picture changes. The American linguist Virginia Collier and the educator Wayne Thomas analysed large datasets over many years and concluded that students in well-implemented dual-language programmes typically reached parity with monolingual peers by around the fifth or sixth grade, and often surpassed them later. Crucially, the programmes that worked best were those that gave sustained, high-quality instruction in both languages rather than rushing children into the majority tongue.

Beyond test scores, bilingual education offers social and emotional benefits. Language is intimately tied to identity, and a school that values a child's home language sends a powerful message that the child's family and culture belong in the classroom. This can improve self-esteem and reduce the alienation that many minority students feel. Bilingual pupils also develop what might be called perspective-taking: the ability to shift between different linguistic and cultural frames. In a dual-language classroom, children learn to negotiate meaning with peers who see the world differently, an experience that can foster empathy and reduce prejudice. Educators report that such classrooms often develop a distinctive atmosphere of mutual respect.

The economic case is increasingly persuasive in a globalised world. Companies routinely operate across borders and value employees who can communicate with clients and colleagues in more than one language. Fluency in a second language opens access to a wider range of universities, jobs and markets. Some studies have found a modest but measurable wage premium associated with bilingualism, particularly in service and diplomatic occupations. At a national level, governments in countries such as Singapore and Switzerland have long treated multilingualism as a strategic asset, while the European Union actively promotes language learning through programmes such as Erasmus. In this view, bilingual education is not a concession to minorities but an investment in human capital.

Critics nonetheless raise legitimate concerns. One common worry is that dividing instructional time between two languages reduces the time available for each, potentially leaving pupils weaker in both. Another is that programmes may be politically contentious: in the United States, 'English-only' movements have argued that public schools should prioritise a single common language, fearing that bilingual education encourages separation. There is also the practical problem of resources. Effective dual-language programmes require teachers who are fluent in both languages, appropriate materials in each, and careful coordination of the curriculum. Such teachers are scarce and often poorly paid, and many schools lack the funds to recruit them. Where programmes are under-resourced, results can be disappointing, which in turn fuels political opposition.

The home environment is another critical factor. Research consistently shows that children benefit when parents continue to speak and read to them in their strongest language, even if that language is not the language of instruction. A rich vocabulary in the first language provides a foundation on which second-language learning can build. Unfortunately, some families are persuaded that they should switch exclusively to the majority language at home, a decision that can impoverish the child's linguistic input and weaken family communication. Schools that involve parents — explaining the value of the home language and offering bilingual reading materials — tend to achieve better outcomes than those that leave families to navigate the system alone.

Implementation therefore matters more than ideology. The most successful programmes share several features: a clear plan for how and when each language will be used, highly qualified teachers, sufficient instructional time in both languages, and assessment that measures proficiency in each. They also avoid treating bilingual pupils as a homogeneous group, recognising that a child born in the country with one minority-language parent has different needs from a recent immigrant with interrupted schooling. Flexible grouping, extra language support and regular monitoring help ensure that no child falls behind. These requirements are demanding, but they are not insurmountable, and countries that have invested in them often report strong results.

In conclusion, the once widespread belief that bilingualism hinders education has been largely abandoned by researchers. When programmes are well designed and adequately resourced, bilingual education can enhance executive function, support literacy, improve academic attainment and nurture social understanding. Its benefits extend beyond the classroom into the workplace and into the fabric of a diverse society. The challenges — political resistance, teacher shortages and uneven implementation — are genuine, but they argue for better programmes rather than for a return to the old assumption that a single language is the only path to success. Two tongues, it turns out, can indeed make one mind more capable.

questions.question: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Children should be punished for speaking their home language in school
Bilingual education is too expensive for most school systems
The majority language should always be the only language of instruction
Well-designed bilingual education offers cognitive, academic and social benefits despite real challenges
questions.explanation: 全文先回顾双语曾被视作问题的历史，再系统论述认知控制、神经证据、读写能力、学业、社会情感与经济收益，最后承认政治与资源挑战并主张改进项目，故主旨为 D。A 是作者明确否定的旧做法；B 只是挑战之一，并非主旨；C 与全文倡导双语的立场相反。

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the Stroop task used to demonstrate?
options: That bilingual children have larger vocabularies than monolinguals
That bilingual children show better attentional control
That minority languages should be taught at home rather than at school
That reading skills develop only after the age of six
questions.explanation: 第3段描述 Stroop 任务：儿童需说出墨水的颜色而非读出词义，双语者更能抑制自动阅读的倾向，显示更高效的注意控制，故选 B。A 文中未用该实验证明词汇量；C 与实验内容无关；D 未提及年龄与阅读的关系。

questions.question: The phrase 'metalinguistic awareness' in paragraph 5 most probably refers to
options: The belief that one language is superior to another
The ability to learn several languages at the same time
An understanding that words are arbitrary symbols that can be analysed
A preference for reading in the majority language
questions.explanation: 第5段将 metalinguistic awareness 定义为'understanding of language as a system that can be analysed and manipulated'，并说儿童知道同一物体可有两种名称便更易理解词语是任意符号，故选 C。A 与原文无关；B 只是多语学习，并非该术语含义；D 原文未提及。

questions.question: What can be inferred about early studies of bilingual pupils' test scores?
options: They were methodologically flawed and did not compare equivalent groups
They proved that bilingualism permanently lowers intelligence
They were conducted mainly in dual-language immersion schools
They showed that bilingual pupils always outperformed monolinguals
questions.explanation: 第6段指出早期研究显示双语学生分数较低，但未能控制社会经济地位，且只用多数语言施测；当研究者比较条件相当的对象时结论改变，故可推断早期研究有方法缺陷、未比较对等群体，选 A。B 与作者结论相反；C 原文未说；D 与'早期分数较低'矛盾。

questions.question: What is the author's attitude towards 'English-only' movements?
options: The author fully endorses their goals
The author considers them the greatest obstacle to bilingualism
The author treats their concerns as entirely baseless
The author acknowledges they are politically contentious but implies better programmes are the answer
questions.explanation: 第8段称双语项目'politically contentious'并提到 English-only 运动的担忧，末段主张以改进项目、而非回到单一语言假设来回应，故作者承认争议但主张靠更好的项目解决，选 D。A 与作者立场相反；B 夸大其词，作者未称其为最大障碍；C 与作者承认合理关切不符。

questions.question: What advice would the author most likely give to parents of bilingual children?
options: Stop speaking the home language so the child can focus
Continue speaking and reading in the language they know best
Avoid reading aloud because it confuses the child
Send the child to a submersion classroom as early as possible
questions.explanation: 第9段明确指出孩子受益于父母继续用最擅长的语言交谈和朗读，即使该语言不是教学语言，少数语言词汇能为第二语言学习奠基，故选 B。A 与原文相反，作者批评放弃母语的做法；C 与原文鼓励朗读相悖；D 原文并未推荐沉浸 submersion 模式。

title: The Restorative Power of Sleep
source: Adapted from neuroscience and sleep medicine publications
description: 睡眠对认知功能与身体健康的作用
content:
For most of human history, sleep was understood as a passive state — a period in which the body switched off and the mind went quiet. Modern science has overturned this picture. Sleep is now recognised as a highly active biological process, during which the brain reorganises information, the body repairs tissue and a host of hormonal systems are recalibrated. Far from being a luxury or a sign of laziness, it is one of the most consequential behaviours we engage in. Yet in industrialised societies, sleep has been steadily eroded, squeezed between the demands of work, education and entertainment. This passage examines how sleep is regulated, what it does for the brain and body, and what happens when it is insufficient.

Two interacting systems govern when we sleep. The first is the circadian rhythm, an internal clock of roughly twenty-four hours centred in a region of the brain called the suprachiasmatic nucleus. This clock is synchronised primarily by light: exposure to daylight in the morning suppresses the hormone melatonin and signals alertness, while the onset of darkness allows melatonin to rise and prepares the body for rest. The second system is sleep pressure, which builds up during wakefulness as adenosine, a chemical byproduct of neural activity, accumulates in the brain. The longer we are awake, the stronger the pressure to sleep. Caffeine works largely by blocking adenosine receptors, which is why a cup of coffee can mask tiredness without removing the underlying need for sleep. Together, these two systems explain why we feel sleepy at night and why an all-nighter leaves us impaired even if we eventually feel alert again.

Sleep itself is not uniform. It cycles through distinct stages, repeating roughly every ninety minutes. Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep begins with light stages and progresses to deep slow-wave sleep, in which brain activity slows dramatically and the body is least responsive to external stimuli. Rapid-eye-movement sleep, or REM, occurs later in the cycle; the brain becomes highly active, resembling wakefulness, while most voluntary muscles are temporarily paralysed. This is the stage most associated with vivid dreaming. A typical night contains four to six cycles, with deep sleep predominating early in the night and REM sleep becoming longer towards morning. The architecture of sleep matters as much as its total duration, since different stages appear to serve different functions.

The most thoroughly studied function of sleep is its role in memory. During slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus — a seahorse-shaped structure essential for forming new memories — repeatedly replays patterns of neural activity that occurred during the day. This replay is thought to transfer information to the cortex for long-term storage, a process called consolidation. Studies have shown that participants who sleep after learning a list of paired words recall significantly more than those who stay awake for the same period. REM sleep appears to contribute differently, particularly to procedural memory — the memory of how to perform tasks — and to emotional memory. One influential experiment found that sleeping after practising a finger-tapping sequence improved speed and accuracy, an effect not seen in those who remained awake. These findings have led researchers to describe sleep not as a pause in learning but as a crucial phase of it.

Sleep also supports the kind of higher-level thinking that neuroscience calls insight. The brain, freed from the constraints of immediate sensory input, can form new associations between ideas that were kept separate during waking hours. The chemist Friedrich Kekulé reportedly discovered the ring structure of benzene after dreaming of a snake biting its own tail, and the composer Robert Louis Stevenson is said to have drawn on dreams for the plot of 'Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde'. The phenomenon may depend on REM sleep, which allows loose combinations of ideas that waking logic would reject.

The consequences of sleep loss are most obvious in cognition. A single night of deprivation impairs attention, working memory and reaction time, and increases the likelihood of microsleeps — brief lapses of several seconds in which a person is effectively unconscious. These effects are comparable to those of alcohol intoxication. This is why shift workers and sleep-deprived drivers pose a serious risk: after twenty-four hours without sleep, reaction times can be as impaired as with a blood alcohol concentration above the legal driving limit. Chronic restriction is no less concerning. Adolescents who consistently get too little sleep perform worse at school, partly because sleepiness reduces the ability to concentrate and to consolidate what they have learned. Remarkably, many people who are chronically sleep-deprived report feeling adapted to it, even though objective tests continue to show significant impairment.

The physical consequences are equally significant. Sleep helps regulate the immune system: during sleep, the body produces more of certain immune cells and antibodies, which is why recovery from illness is often accompanied by a desire to sleep. Sleep also influences metabolism. ItAdjusts the balance of two hormones, leptin and ghrelin, which respectively signal fullness and hunger. Sleep restriction lowers leptin and raises ghrelin, increasing appetite, particularly for carbohydrate-rich foods. This helps explain the consistent epidemiological association between short sleep and obesity. In addition, insufficient sleep is linked to impaired glucose tolerance and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, probably because it increases insulin resistance. These findings have led some researchers to describe sleep as a pillar of metabolic health, alongside diet and exercise.

Cardiovascular health is also affected. Large prospective studies have found that people who habitually sleep fewer than six hours a night have a higher incidence of hypertension, coronary heart disease and stroke than those who sleep seven or eight hours. Several mechanisms may be involved: sleep deprivation raises levels of stress hormones such as cortisol, increases inflammation and disrupts the normal night-time dip in blood pressure that the heart needs to recover.
